output.text_response:
# Locality Guide: New York City (1700s Colonial Period)

## Jurisdiction Overview

New Amsterdam was founded as a Dutch colony in 1626, seized by the English in 1664 and renamed New York City. By the 1700s it operated as the seat of New York Province under British colonial rule. The city corresponded broadly to **New York County (Manhattan)** — the five modern boroughs did not yet exist; Kings, Queens, Richmond, and Westchester were distinct jurisdictions with their own record series.

**Key ethnic groups:** Dutch (from the New Amsterdam era), English (dominant after 1664), Huguenot (French Protestant), Sephardic Jewish (present from 1654), and enslaved Africans.

**Key historical disruption:** British military occupation (1776–1783) disrupted civic record-keeping. Records from this period have gaps.

---

## Record Types

### Church Records *(Most Important for This Period)*

There were **no civil vital records** (births, marriages, deaths) in the 1700s — New York State did not require civil registration until 1880. Churches are the only vital-event record source for the entire colonial period.

| Denomination | Records Available | Where Held |
|---|---|---|
| **Dutch Reformed (Collegiate)** | Registers from 1639; 1700–1776 volume digitized on FamilySearch (DGS 007733180, 211 images) — **browse-only, in Dutch, 0% indexed** | FamilySearch; NYGBS |
| **Anglican / Trinity Church** | Baptisms, marriages, burials from 1697 | Trinity Church Archives; published abstracts |
| **Presbyterian, Lutheran, French Reformed (Huguenot)** | Varying survival | NYGBS; New-York Historical Society |
| **Shearith Israel (Jewish)** | Congregation and cemetery records from 1654 | American Jewish Historical Society |

> **Critical warning:** The Dutch Reformed register must be browsed page by page and read in early modern Dutch script. It is the most extensive colonial baptism series in the city — but it requires either Dutch-language skills or a translator.

FamilySearch collection: **New York, Church Records, 1640–1940** (collection 1469062).

---

### Probate Records

- **Jurisdiction quirk:** In colonial New York, probate was handled by the **Prerogative Court of New York** at the *provincial* level — NOT at the county level. Search there before assuming a will doesn't exist.
- After 1778, the Surrogate's Court of New York County took over.
- The New-York Historical Society published the *Abstracts of Wills* series — an essential finding aid for 1700s wills.
- FamilySearch collection: **New York, Probate Records, 1629–1971** (collection 1542780) — digitized and searchable.

---

### Land Records

- Land patents and grants were issued by the Governor of New York Province on behalf of the Crown.
- FamilySearch collection: **New York, Land Records, 1630–1975** (collection 2078654) — digitized and searchable.
- Original colonial patents held at the **New York State Archives** (Albany); city lot deeds held at the NYC Department of Finance (Register's Office).

---

### Tax / Assessment Records (Census Substitutes)

- Ward-level assessments of real and personal estate served as the best substitute for a census (the first federal census was 1790 — after the colonial period).
- FamilySearch collection: **New York, Tax Assessment Rolls, 1799–1804** (collection 1678432) — covers the very end of this period.
- Earlier ward assessment lists are physical/microfilm only, held at the **NYC Municipal Archives** and **New York State Archives**.

---

### Military Records

| Conflict | Record Types | Where Held |
|---|---|---|
| Queen Anne's War (1702–1713); King George's War (1744–1748); French and Indian War (1754–1763) | Colonial militia rolls by ward/township | NYS Archives; published in part |
| Revolutionary War (1775–1783) | Service records, pension files, state muster rolls | NARA; Fold3 (subscription); NYS Archives |

---

### Newspapers

- **New-York Gazette** (founded 1725) and **New-York Weekly Journal** (founded 1733) are the primary papers.
- Content: marriage and death notices, legal notices, runaway servant/slave advertisements (naming individuals), ship arrivals.
- **Chronicling America** (free): select digitized colonial issues.
- **Newspapers.com** (subscription): broader access.
- New-York Historical Society holds extensive microfilm runs.

---

### Cemetery Records

- **Trinity Church churchyard** (burials from 1697), **St. Paul's Chapel churchyard**, and **Shearith Israel cemetery on Chatham Square** (oldest surviving Jewish burial ground in the U.S., from 1683) are the most significant.
- Sexton's burial registers for Trinity Church and others survive at respective church archives; transcriptions published by NYGBS.
- FindAGrave.com lists many colonial-era headstones. Note: headstone attrition in lower Manhattan is severe due to urban redevelopment.

---

### Immigration Records

- Systematic passenger manifests were not required until 1820 — colonial-era arrival records are sparse.
- Best evidence for immigrant origins comes from **church membership records** (which often note a member's place of origin) and published *New York Historical Manuscripts*.
- Pre-1906 naturalizations are in court records (Mayor's Court, provincial courts) or Acts of the Provincial Legislature.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online

| Repository | Key Collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Church records (coll. 1469062), Land records (coll. 2078654), Probate records (coll. 1542780), Tax rolls 1799–1804 (coll. 1678432), Dutch Reformed browse volume DGS 007733180 | Free |
| **Ancestry.com** | US Federal Census (from 1790 only); NY church and probate transcriptions | Subscription |
| **Fold3.com** | Revolutionary War service records and pensions | Subscription |
| **Newspapers.com** | Historical NY newspapers | Subscription |
| **Chronicling America** (loc.gov) | Select colonial-era NY papers | Free |
| **FindAGrave.com** | Colonial burial ground inscriptions | Free |

### Physical Repositories

| Repository | Key Holdings |
|---|---|
| **New York City Municipal Archives** (31 Chambers St.) | Colonial city records, assessment lists, Mayor's Court minute books |
| **New York State Archives** (Albany) | Colonial Manuscripts, Prerogative Court probate, provincial land patents, militia rolls |
| **New-York Historical Society** | Church record transcriptions, *Abstracts of Wills*, newspaper runs, manumission records |
| **New York Genealogical & Biographical Society (NYGBS)** | Church record transcriptions, published vital record indexes |
| **Trinity Church Archives** | Registers from 1697; vestry minutes; churchyard inscriptions (by appointment) |
| **American Jewish Historical Society** | Shearith Israel records; Jewish community history |
| **British National Archives (Kew)** | Colonial Office papers (NY Province); Admiralty records with some ship lists |

---

## Known Record Losses

- Many colonial civic records were lost or displaced during British occupation (1776–1783).
- Some early Dutch Reformed records from the 17th century do not survive.
- Urban redevelopment across lower Manhattan has destroyed many colonial-era church and burial grounds.

---

## Key Research Tips

1. **Start with the church, not a courthouse.** Identify which denomination the family attended (Dutch = Dutch Reformed; English = Anglican/Trinity; French = Huguenot/French Reformed) and go directly to that congregation's registers.

2. **Dutch naming customs are tricky.** Dutch colonial families used a patronymic system — a child's surname was the father's first name plus "-sz" (sons) or "-dr" (daughters). Fixed hereditary surnames emerged gradually across the 1700s. Don't assume surname consistency across generations.

3. **Probate is at the provincial level, not the county.** Search the published *Abstracts of Wills* (NYGBS / New-York Historical Society) and FamilySearch collection 1542780 before concluding no will exists.

4. **Ward identification matters.** Tax lists, assessment rolls, and some church records are organized by city ward. Knowing which ward a family lived in focuses all subsequent searches.

5. **The 1790 federal census is your earliest census bridge.** Use it to identify household heads and work backward through church registers, tax lists, and probate records.

6. **Very little is name-indexed online.** Only 1 digitized volume for this period appeared in FamilySearch's volume index, and it requires reading Dutch. Most colonial-era NYC research involves physical or microfilm archives, or published transcription projects from the NYGBS.

7. **For enslaved ancestors:** Wills, estate inventories, and manumission records at the New-York Historical Society are the best documentary sources. Church records occasionally record baptisms of enslaved individuals by name.

# Locality Guide: New York City (1700s Colonial Period)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** New Amsterdam was founded as a Dutch colony in 1626; seized by the English in 1664 and renamed New York City. By the 1700s it operated as the seat of New York Province under British colonial rule.
- **County / administrative structure:** The city corresponded broadly to New York County (Manhattan). The five modern boroughs did not yet exist in their current form; Kings, Queens, Richmond, and Westchester counties were distinct jurisdictions.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** New York Province (British Crown colony), superseded by the State of New York after 1777.
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the tool for this specific place and time window. Contemporary estimates place the colonial city at roughly 5,000 in 1700, growing to around 25,000 by the 1780s.
- **Economy:** Major commercial seaport; merchant trade, shipping, warehousing, artisan crafts, and domestic service. The city was the commercial hub of the mid-Atlantic colonies.
- **Ethnic composition:** Dutch families (many from the original New Amsterdam era), English settlers (dominant after 1664), Huguenot (French Protestant) refugees, Jewish families (Sephardic community present from 1654), and enslaved Africans who appear in church records, inventories, and manumission documents.
- **Religious denominations:** Dutch Reformed (oldest continuous records), Anglican/Church of England (Trinity Church founded 1697), Presbyterian, Lutheran, French Reformed (Huguenot), Jewish (Shearith Israel congregation), Quaker, and Baptist.
- **Key historical events:** The English takeover (1664) creates a record-language shift from Dutch to English. The 1741 "Great Negro Plot" trials generate court records. British occupation during the Revolutionary War (1776-1783) disrupts local administration. The city briefly served as the first U.S. capital (1789-1790).

## Boundary changes

- Through the whole of the 1700s, New York City was effectively coextensive with New York County (the island of Manhattan). Kings, Queens, Westchester, and Richmond were separate counties with their own court and church record series.
- No county subdivision occurred within New York County itself during the 1700s — boundary changes that affected research are those of adjoining counties, not of the city itself.
- Records generated before 1664 are in Dutch and were made under Dutch colonial authority; after 1664, English-language records predominate, though Dutch Reformed church records continued in Dutch well into the 18th century.
- The provincial government dissolved in 1776; from that point forward, the State of New York assumed jurisdiction over record-keeping systems.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** There was no civil (government-mandated) registration of births, marriages, or deaths anywhere in New York in the 1700s. No statewide civil registration existed. New York State did not require statewide registration until 1880 (with spotty compliance extending into the early 1900s). The FamilySearch Wiki pages for New York Vital Records, Church Records, and related topics returned only a generic fallback page in this session rather than New York-specific content, so no specific early local registration date can be confirmed from fetched pages.
- **What exists:** For 1700-1800, there is no civil registration series. All vital-event recording was done by churches. See Church Records below.
- **Where held:** N/A for civil registration in this period.
- **Gaps:** The entire 1700s is a gap for civil vital records — this is the normal condition for this period, not a loss.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism, marriage, and burial registers are the primary vital-event sources for the entire colonial period. See Church Records below.

### Church records

This is the single most important record category for 1700s New York City research. Churches were the only institutions recording births/baptisms, marriages, and deaths/burials for most of the population.

- **Dutch Reformed Church (Collegiate Church):** The oldest continuous record series in New York City, beginning in 1639 and running through the colonial period. FamilySearch has digitized 1 volume covering **1700-1776** (image group 007733180, 211 images). This volume is **browse-only** — it has 0% name-indexing and is not full-text searchable. Critically, the records are in **Dutch**, requiring the researcher to read early modern Dutch script. This is the most extensive colonial baptism series in the city. Source: `volume_search` result. The broader FamilySearch collection "New York, Church Records, 1640-1940" (collection 1469062) also encompasses church records for this period.
- **Trinity Church (Anglican/Episcopal):** Founded 1697. Registers of baptisms, marriages, and burials from 1697 onward are among the best-documented Anglican records in colonial North America. The church has published abstracts; originals are held at Trinity Church Archives, Broadway at Wall Street, Manhattan.
- **Presbyterian, Lutheran, French Reformed (Huguenot), and other denominations:** Maintained their own registers. Quality and survival vary. The New York Genealogical & Biographical Society (NYGBS) and New-York Historical Society hold or have microfilmed many of these. Source: wiki_search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records.
- **Jewish records (Congregation Shearith Israel):** The oldest Jewish congregation in North America (est. 1654). Cemetery and congregation records survive; held at the congregation and at the American Jewish Historical Society.
- **Language:** Dutch Reformed records through much of the 1700s are in Dutch. Anglican, Presbyterian, and French Reformed records are in English or French respectively.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (digitized volume above); Trinity Church Archives; NYGBS; New-York Historical Society; individual denominational archives.

### Census records

- **Federal census:** The first federal census was 1790 — outside the colonial period entirely. It does not cover the 1700s. New York City appears in the 1790 census (the earliest available), which is indexed and broadly available online.
- **Colonial enumerations:** New York Province conducted various head-counts and militia musters during the 1700s, but these are not full household censuses. Some survive in the New York State Archives as colonial manuscripts.
- **Tax and assessment lists:** Ward-level tax assessment lists survive for some years and serve as census substitutes. The FamilySearch collection "New York, Tax Assessment Rolls of Real and Personal Estates, 1799-1804" (collection 1678432, date range 1799-1804) touches the very end of the period. Earlier ward assessment lists are held at the New York City Municipal Archives and the New York State Archives.
- **Access:** The 1799-1804 tax rolls are digitized on FamilySearch (collection 1678432). Earlier colonial assessment lists are largely physical or microfilm only.

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, letters of administration, guardianship papers. In colonial New York, probate was handled by the **Prerogative Court of New York** (provincial level), not at the county level — a critical quirk. After 1778, the Surrogate's Court of New York County took over.
- **Published abstracts:** The New-York Historical Society published the *Abstracts of Wills* series, covering colonial-era wills proved before the Prerogative Court. This is an essential finding aid for the 1700s. Source: wiki_search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "New York, Probate Records, 1629-1971" (collection 1542780) covers this period. It is digitized and searchable.
- **Mayor's Court:** The Mayor's Court of New York City handled civil disputes and some naturalization matters throughout the colonial period. Court minute books survive and are held at the New York City Municipal Archives and the New York State Archives.
- **Testate vs. intestate:** Persons who left wills (testate) are found in the will books of the Prerogative Court; those who died intestate generated letters of administration in the same court.
- **Where held:** New York State Archives (Albany); New York City Municipal Archives; New-York Historical Society (published abstracts); FamilySearch (collection 1542780).

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (not the later rectangular survey system).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** During the colonial period, land patents and grants were issued by the Governor of New York Province on behalf of the Crown. The Secretary of State's office maintained the patent books. The FamilySearch collection "New York, Land Records, 1630-1975" (collection 2078654) covers this period and is digitized and searchable.
- **Types:** Royal patents, deeds of conveyance, mortgages. Large land grants ("manors") characterized some areas outside the city proper; within the city, lot deeds and conveyances are the relevant records.
- **Land-grant records:** Original colonial patents are held at the New York State Archives. City lot deeds are in the New York County Register's office (now part of NYC Department of Finance).
- **Where held:** New York State Archives; NYC Department of Finance (Register's Office); FamilySearch (collection 2078654).

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** Queen Anne's War (1702-1713); King George's War (1744-1748); French and Indian War (1754-1763); American Revolutionary War (1775-1783).
- **Record types:** Colonial militia rolls (province-level, listing men of military age and their wards/townships); Revolutionary War service records and pension files.
- **Colonial militia rolls:** Survive for some years in the New York State Archives and have been published in part. They are useful for identifying male residents. Source: wiki_search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records.
- **Revolutionary War records:** NARA holds Continental Army service records and pension files. Fold3.com (subscription) provides online access. The New York State Archives holds state-level muster rolls.
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington, D.C. and regional facilities); New York State Archives; Fold3 (online, subscription); FamilySearch (some digitized pension indexes).

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** Trinity Church churchyard (oldest surviving in Manhattan, burials from 1697); St. Paul's Chapel churchyard; Shearith Israel (Spanish-Portuguese Jewish) cemetery on Chatham Square (oldest surviving Jewish burial ground in the U.S., from 1683); Dutch Reformed churchyard (largely disappeared); various dissenting congregation yards.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave.com lists many colonial-era headstones where inscriptions survive. Headstone attrition in lower Manhattan is severe — many colonial-era stones were lost to urban development.
- **Physical records:** Sexton's burial registers for Trinity Church and some others survive; held at respective church archives. Transcriptions have been published.
- **Where held:** Trinity Church Archives; individual church records; New-York Historical Society (published transcriptions); FindAGrave.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** The *New-York Gazette* (founded 1725, the city's first newspaper) and the *New-York Weekly Journal* (founded 1733) are the primary 1700s papers. Additional titles appeared in the second half of the century.
- **Content value:** Marriage notices, death notices, legal notices (estate administrations, land sales), runaway servant and slave advertisements (which name individuals), and ship arrivals naming passengers.
- **Where held:** Digitized issues are available through the Library of Congress "Chronicling America" portal (chroniclingamerica.loc.gov) and through Newspapers.com (subscription). The New-York Historical Society holds extensive original runs on microfilm.
- **Note:** These papers did not publish systematic vital-event notices; notices were placed voluntarily and capture only a subset of events.

### Immigration and emigration records

- **Relevant ports:** New York Harbor was the primary port of entry for the city. Passenger lists for colonial-era arrivals are sparse and incomplete — systematic manifests were not required until 1820.
- **Record types:** Some ship lists survive in colonial manuscripts and British Admiralty records. Naturalization records in the Mayor's Court and the Provincial Supreme Court document the formal process.
- **Colonial-era arrivals:** Many Dutch, Huguenot, and other immigrant arrivals in the early-to-mid 1700s can be partially traced through church membership records (the congregation admitted and recorded new members, often noting their place of origin) and through the published *New York Historical Manuscripts* series.
- **Naturalization:** Pre-1906 naturalizations are in court records (Mayor's Court, provincial courts). Many colonial-era "naturalizations" were actually Acts of the Provincial Legislature — published and indexed separately.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists for this period are fragmentary. Church membership and land records often provide the most reliable immigration evidence.
- **Where held:** NARA; New York State Archives; New-York Historical Society; British National Archives (Kew) for colonial-era Admiralty and provincial records.

### Tax records

- **Types:** Ward-level assessments of real and personal estates; poll taxes.
- **Date range:** Some assessments survive from the 1690s onward. The FamilySearch collection 1678432 covers 1799-1804. Earlier lists are held in the New York City Municipal Archives and at the New York State Archives in the colonial manuscript series.
- **Where held:** New York City Municipal Archives; New York State Archives; FamilySearch (collection 1678432 for 1799-1804).
- **Substitute value:** For years with no census, tax lists establish a person's presence in a specific ward, their taxable property, and sometimes their occupation.

### Other record types

- **New York Colonial Manuscripts:** The New York State Archives holds the main body of colonial government records — governor's council minutes, provincial secretary's papers, Indian treaties, and more. These are indexed in published calendar volumes ("Calendar of New York Colonial Manuscripts"). An essential repository for residents who appear in any official capacity.
- **Town and county histories:** 19th-century published histories of New York City (e.g., Valentine's *Manual of the Corporation of the City of New York*, annual volumes from the 1840s-1860s) reprint colonial records, lists of officeholders, and biographical notices that preserve information no longer available elsewhere.
- **Manumission records:** The New York Manumission Society (founded 1785) and related court documents track enslaved and freed Black New Yorkers; held at the New-York Historical Society.
- **Indentures and apprenticeship records:** The City recorded indentures of apprentices; some survive in the Municipal Archives.

---

## Records NOT online

The following are known to exist for 1700s New York City but have no online-searchable presence (or only fragmentary online coverage):

- Pre-1799 ward tax assessment lists (held physically at NYC Municipal Archives and NYS Archives)
- Mayor's Court minute books (colonial period)
- Colonial militia rolls (beyond what has been published in print)
- Most individual church registers outside the Dutch Reformed collection on FamilySearch — many denominations' original registers are in church archives only
- Indentures and apprenticeship records at the Municipal Archives
- Huguenot congregation registers (partial transcriptions only)
- Lutheran church registers

---

## Known record losses

- Many colonial-era civic records were lost or displaced during the British military occupation of New York City (1776-1783). The British used City Hall and other public buildings for military purposes, and record continuity was disrupted.
- Some early Dutch Reformed church records from the 17th century do not survive; the 1700-1776 volume on FamilySearch represents what has been preserved.
- Urban redevelopment across lower Manhattan has destroyed many colonial-era church and burial grounds, eliminating physical artifacts that might have corroborated or substituted for documentary records.
- No substitute fully compensates for the occupation-era civic record gap; church records, published newspaper notices, and provincial government records at Albany are the best alternatives for 1776-1783.

---

## Research tips

- **No civil vital records exist for the 1700s.** Church baptism, marriage, and burial registers are the only vital-event records for this period. Begin with the church the family attended — determined by ethnic background (Dutch families = Dutch Reformed; English = Anglican/Trinity; Huguenots = French Reformed). Source: wiki_search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records.
- **The Dutch Reformed register (DGS 007733180) must be browsed image by image in Dutch.** It is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable. If your ancestors were Dutch or Dutch Reformed, this is the single most important digitized source — but it requires reading early modern Dutch script (or engaging a translator).
- **Probate for the 1700s was at the provincial level, not the county level.** The Prerogative Court of New York (not a county Surrogate's Court) handled all colonial-era probate. Search the published *Abstracts of Wills* (New-York Historical Society) and FamilySearch collection 1542780 before assuming a will does not exist. Source: wiki_search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records.
- **Ward-level research is essential.** The city was divided into wards (the number grew over the century). Tax lists, assessment rolls, and some church records are organized by ward rather than alphabetically. Knowing which ward a family lived in focuses searches considerably.
- **The 1790 federal census is the earliest available.** It captures the post-colonial generation and serves as a bridge back to colonial records. Use it to identify household heads, then work backward through church registers, tax lists, and probate records.
- **Search adjoining county records.** Families in Brooklyn (Kings County), Jamaica (Queens County), and Staten Island (Richmond County) generated records in those separate county jurisdictions — not in New York County. If a family moved between boroughs-to-be, records will be split across different county archives. The neighboring-county table for New York County was not returned by the FamilySearch wiki page tool in this session, so a full neighbor list cannot be confirmed from fetched pages, but Kings, Queens, Richmond, and Westchester were the immediate neighbors.
- **Dutch naming customs:** Dutch colonial families used a patronymic system (a child's surname was the father's first name plus "-sz" for sons and "-dr" for daughters) that was gradually replaced by fixed hereditary surnames across the 1700s. A family named "Jansen" in 1720 may have grandchildren with the surname "Van Der Berg" or a completely different fixed surname. Do not assume surname consistency across generations for families of Dutch origin. The FamilySearch New York Naming Customs page returned only a generic fallback in this session; consult the NYGBS directly for guidance.
- **The New York Genealogical and Biographical Record** (the NYGBS journal, published since 1870) has indexed and transcribed thousands of colonial church registers, wills, and cemetery inscriptions. Consult its cumulative indexes before writing off a source as unavailable online.
- **For enslaved ancestors:** Wills, estate inventories, and manumission records at the New-York Historical Society are among the best documentary sources. The 1790 and 1800 censuses enumerate enslaved persons only as numbers, not names, in slaveholder households. Church records occasionally record baptisms of enslaved individuals by name.

---

## Summary for user

New York City in the 1700s was under British colonial rule for most of the century, and its records reflect that dual Dutch-English heritage. There were no government birth, marriage, or death certificates for this period — those did not exist anywhere in New York until the 1800s. The records that survive are church registers (especially the Dutch Reformed church, whose colonial registers are on FamilySearch but must be browsed page by page in Dutch), land deeds and patents held at the New York State Archives in Albany, probate records from the provincial-level Prerogative Court (not a county courthouse), ward tax assessment lists, colonial government manuscripts, court minute books, and newspaper notices. The most important physical repositories are the New York City Municipal Archives, the New York State Archives, the New-York Historical Society, and Trinity Church's own archives. The biggest practical caution is that very little of this material is name-indexed online — only 1 digitized volume covering this period appeared in FamilySearch's volume index, and it requires reading Dutch — so most colonial-era New York City research involves visiting or corresponding with physical archives or working through published transcription projects like the NYGBS's church-record series.

With this survey in hand, the next step is building a research plan that sequences the most likely sources for your specific family — starting with identifying the church they attended and working backward through its registers, then cross-referencing with probate and land records.

output.text_response:
# Virginia Revolutionary War Records Guide (1775–1783)

Here is a comprehensive locality guide for tracing families connected to Virginia military service and wartime activities:

---

## Jurisdiction Overview

Virginia was the most populous state during the Revolution (~747,000 by 1790). Its county formation was rapid — a family could appear in entirely different county records within just a few years without having moved. **Always identify the specific county at the specific date of each event.**

⚠️ **Important boundary note:** Kentucky County was part of Virginia until 1792, and West Virginia didn't separate until 1863. Ancestors in those modern states require Virginia records for this period.

---

## Key Military Record Types

### 1. Continental Army Records (National Archives — NARA)
- **Service records** — RG 93: Confirm enlistment, unit, and officer names
- **Pension & bounty-land applications** — RG 15 (**start here!**): Sworn affidavits describing service, battles, age, birthplace, family members, and neighbors who vouched for the veteran. Widow's files often add maiden names, marriage dates, and children's names. Available on Fold3 (subscription).
- **FamilySearch collection:** Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783 (ID 1945678) — indexed + images at [familysearch.org](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1945678)

### 2. Virginia Militia Records (separate from Continental records)
- Held at the **Library of Virginia**, Richmond
- Many men served in both militia *and* the Continental Line at different times — search both

### 3. Bounty Land Warrants
- Virginia issued land grants in the **Virginia Military District of Ohio** to veterans
- Records at the Library of Virginia and Ohio State Archives
- FamilySearch image group **005301447** (Revolutionary War land bounty warrants, 1779–1800; 341 images — browse-only, not indexed)
- Often names the county of residence at the time of application — a valuable locating clue

---

## Critical Record Substitutes (Due to Record Losses)

### ⚠️ The 1790 Virginia Census Was Destroyed
The British burned Washington in 1814, destroying Virginia's 1790 census. The primary substitutes are:

- **1782–1783 county personal property tax lists** — Virginia's most complete early enumeration, listing heads of household by county. FamilySearch collection: Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850 (ID 1456723); also image group **005301449** (full-text searchable, 87 images)
- **1783 Virginia state census** — fragmentary, survives for some counties at the Library of Virginia

---

## Supporting Record Types

| Record Type | Key Source | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Church registers** (Anglican/Baptist/Presbyterian) | FamilySearch collection ID 1598230 (1680–1929) | Free, indexed |
| **County court order books** | Image group 005301448 — Augusta County, 1775–1795 (61% indexed) | FamilySearch browse |
| **Land, wills & marriage bonds** | FamilySearch collection ID 1734285 (1600–1900) | Free, indexed |
| **County court records** | FamilySearch collection ID 2134567 (1650–1920) | Free, indexed |
| **Virginia Gazette newspaper** | Library of Virginia microfilm; some on Chronicling America | Free/subscription |

---

## Major Repositories

| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| **Library of Virginia, Richmond** | Militia records, Land Office patents/grants, tax lists from 1782, county court records, loyalist confiscation records |
| **National Archives (Washington, D.C.)** | Continental Line service records (RG 93), pension/bounty-land files (RG 15) |
| **FamilySearch** | Multiple indexed collections (see above) — free |
| **Fold3** | Digitized NARA pension files and service records — subscription |
| **DAR Library, Washington D.C.** | Compiled service records, grave surveys, lineage papers |
| **Virginia Baptist Historical Society** | Baptist church records |

---

## Research Strategy Tips

1. **Start with pension files, not service records.** Pension applications (NARA RG 15 / Fold3) are far richer genealogically than service records.

2. **Use the 1782–1783 tax lists as your baseline census.** These are the only systematic early enumeration covering the war's end.

3. **Search both Continental Line and militia records.** A man not found in one may appear in the other.

4. **County court order books reveal civilian wartime life.** Even non-serving family members appear for road assignments, militia equipment assessments, tax delinquency, poor relief, and estates.

5. **Anglican vestry records fill the vital-records gap.** No civil birth or death registration existed in Virginia during this period — church registers (FamilySearch collection 1598230) are the closest equivalent.

6. **Loyalist families leave a different trail.** Property confiscation records (held at Library of Virginia) under Virginia's 1779 acts may name family members. Absence from militia musters combined with confiscation records signals Loyalist status.

7. **Virginia is a state-land state.** All land grants came from Virginia's Land Office — the BLM/GLO site does not cover Virginia patents. Search the Library of Virginia's online catalog for these records.

---

## Records Not Yet Fully Online
- Virginia militia records (Library of Virginia; microfilm exists but indexing is incomplete)
- Virginia State Navy records (published in print; not systematically digitized)
- Revolutionary War land bounty warrants, 1779–1800 (images online but browse-only)
- Most Anglican/Episcopal vestry books not yet in FamilySearch collection 1598230
- Virginia's 1783 state census fragments

---

**Bottom line:** Begin with pension files and the 1782–1783 tax lists. Then identify the specific county your ancestor lived in and pull that county's court order books, militia records, and church registers. That combination — pension file + tax list + county court + church record — gives the firmest foundation for Revolutionary War Virginia research.

# Locality Guide: Virginia, United States (1775–1783)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** Virginia was one of the original thirteen colonies; it ratified the U.S. Constitution in 1788 and was already a functioning state government throughout the Revolutionary War period.
- **Administrative center:** Richmond (state capital from 1780; Williamsburg before that).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Commonwealth of Virginia under the new United States government.
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the place_population tool for this period; the 1790 federal census (the earliest surviving) counted approximately 747,000 people in Virginia, making it the most populous state.
- **Economy:** Tobacco cultivation (dominant), mixed farming, iron furnaces, shipbuilding, and trade through ports at Norfolk and Alexandria.
- **Ethnic composition:** English-origin settlers predominating; significant Scots-Irish and German populations in the Shenandoah Valley and western counties; enslaved African Americans constituted a large portion of the population.
- **Religious denominations:** Anglican/Church of England (the established church before disestablishment in 1786), Baptist, Presbyterian, Methodist, Quaker, Lutheran (German-speaking western counties).
- **Key historical events:** Declaration of Independence 1776; Dunmore's Proclamation (1775) offering freedom to enslaved people who escaped to British lines; major campaigns and skirmishes throughout Virginia 1779-1781; Cornwallis's surrender at Yorktown, October 1781; Virginia Military District of Ohio bounty land grants following the war.

## Boundary changes

Virginia during 1775–1783 was far larger than the modern state; Kentucky County was carved from Fincastle County in 1776 and remained part of Virginia until Kentucky statehood in 1792. West Virginia did not become a separate state until 1863. Researchers tracing ancestors in what is today West Virginia or Kentucky must use Virginia records for this period. County formation was rapid during and after the Revolution — a family might appear in one county's records in 1776 and an entirely different county's records by 1783 without having moved. Always identify the specific county at the specific date of the event you are researching.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** Virginia did not have statewide civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths during 1775–1783. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Virginia Vital Records returned only generic content rather than Virginia-specific dates for this period, so no specific statewide date is cited here from a tool result.
- **What exists:** No government-mandated birth or death registration applied to the war years at the county or state level.
- **Marriage bonds and licenses:** Marriage bonds were recorded at the county level throughout the colonial and early statewide period and are among the best surviving vital-record substitutes. These are held at county courthouses and have been extensively microfilmed.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers (Anglican parish registers, Baptist and Presbyterian congregational records) are the primary vital-event sources for this period. The FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929" (collection ID 1598230, date range 1680–1929) is indexed and searchable at [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598230](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598230).

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Anglican (Church of England, reorganized as Episcopal after the Revolution), Baptist, Presbyterian, Methodist, Quaker (Friends meetings), Lutheran. The established Anglican/Episcopal church kept parish registers that are among the most complete surviving vital records for this era.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, vestry minutes (which also record poor relief and road maintenance assignments, naming ordinary community members).
- **Where held:** Many Anglican vestry books and registers are at the Library of Virginia in Richmond, with microfilm copies at FamilySearch. County-level Baptist and Presbyterian congregational records are held variously at denominational archives, local churches, and the Virginia Baptist Historical Society (Richmond). FamilySearch has digitized a substantial number of Virginia church records in collection 1598230.
- **Language:** English.
- **Access:** Collection 1598230 is indexed + images online (name-searchable). Individual vestry records not yet digitized are microfilm or physical only.

### Census records

- **Federal census:** The 1790 federal census for Virginia was destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814 — this is explicitly noted in the FamilySearch Wiki search result at [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands). The earliest surviving Virginia federal census is 1800.
- **Substitute — tax lists:** Virginia county personal property and land tax lists beginning in 1782 are the single most important substitute for the missing 1790 census. FamilySearch has a digitized volume of Virginia state enumerations/tax lists, 1782–1799 (image group 005301449; 87 images; 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable). These lists place a named head of household in a specific county in a specific year, making them essential for tracking families through the war and its immediate aftermath.
- **1783 Virginia state census:** A fragmentary state enumeration survives for some counties from 1783 and is held at the Library of Virginia.

### Military records (PRIMARY FOCUS)

Virginia contributed more soldiers to the Continental Army than any other colony. The FamilySearch Wiki result at [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War) identifies the following:

**FamilySearch indexed collections:**
- "Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783" (collection ID 1945678, date range 1775–1783) — indexed + images online, searchable by name at [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1945678](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1945678).

**Digitized volumes (from volume_search):**
- Image group 005301447 — Revolutionary War land bounty warrants, Virginia, 1779–1800. 341 images. 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable: **browse-only images**. These connect veterans to specific land grants issued by Virginia.
- Image group 005301448 — Augusta County court order books, 1775–1795. 158 images. 61% name-indexed. These county court minutes record militia musters, appointments, and other wartime civil administration.

**National Archives (NARA) — the foundational repository:**
- Continental Line service records and muster rolls: NARA Record Group 93.
- Pension and bounty-land warrant applications: NARA Record Group 15. Pension files are especially valuable — they often contain affidavits by the veteran or widow describing service, age, family members, and place of residence. Many are available through Fold3 (subscription).
- Virginia State Navy records: published separately (ask at the Library of Virginia).

**Virginia militia records** are held at the Library of Virginia in Richmond. These are separate from Continental Line records and cover men who served in county militias rather than the regular Continental Army.

**Bounty land — Virginia Military District of Ohio:** After the war, Virginia granted bounty lands in a reserved district in Ohio to its veterans. Warrant and survey records connecting veterans to these grants are at the Library of Virginia and at the Ohio State Archives (for surveys). Per the FamilySearch Wiki at [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands), these records are at the Virginia State Library and connect veterans to specific land parcels.

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills, inventories, estate administrations, guardianships, county court order books (which record militia and civil wartime activities).
- **Where held:** County courthouses (original records); Library of Virginia (microfilm and some originals); FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900" (collection ID 1734285) — indexed + images online at [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1734285](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1734285).
- **County court order books** (like image group 005301448 above) are especially valuable for the war years: they recorded militia appointments, road assignments, poor relief, and other administrative business naming ordinary residents who never appear in formal legal proceedings.
- **Testate vs. intestate:** Veterans who died during or shortly after the war leaving property are likely to appear in county probate; those dying intestate will have administration records rather than wills.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Virginia is a state-land state; land was granted by Virginia, not the federal government).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The Virginia Land Office issued grants and patents; post-war bounty land warrants for veterans were issued by the Virginia government.
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, patents, surveys, land tax records, bounty land warrants.
- **Where held:** Virginia Land Office records (grants and patents) are at the Library of Virginia. County deed books are at county courthouses. The FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900" (collection ID 1734285) covers land and deed records as well.
- **Tax records as land substitute:** Virginia land tax lists beginning 1782 are at the Library of Virginia and are among the earliest systematic property records covering the war's end.
- **Digitized volume:** Image group 005301447 (Revolutionary War land bounty warrants, 1779–1800; browse-only, 341 images) directly documents veteran land grants.

### Tax records

- **Types:** Personal property tax lists and land tax lists, both beginning 1782 at the county level by state mandate.
- **Date range:** 1782 onward; these are the most complete early coverage.
- **Where held:** Library of Virginia (originals and microfilm); FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850" (collection ID 1456723) — indexed + images online at [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1456723](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1456723). Also accessible as image group 005301449 (state enumerations/tax lists, 1782–1799; full-text searchable, 87 images).
- **Substitute value:** The 1782 and 1783 tax lists are the single best substitute for the destroyed 1790 Virginia census and the only systematic head-of-household enumeration covering the end of the Revolutionary War.

### Cemetery records

- **Coverage:** FindAGrave ([https://www.findagrave.com/](https://www.findagrave.com/)) is the primary online source; coverage of 18th-century markers in Virginia is uneven, as many early grave markers have been lost.
- **Physical records:** No centralized sexton records exist for this era; individual church burial registers (see Church records above) are the best-documented source.
- **Revolutionary War graves:** The DAR (Daughters of the American Revolution) has surveyed and marked many Revolutionary War graves in Virginia; the DAR library in Washington, D.C., holds their records.

### Probate and court records (county court order books)

- **Access:** The county court order books (image group 005301448, Augusta County, 1775–1795) are 61% name-indexed — partially searchable, partially browse-only. The FamilySearch collection "Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920" (collection ID 2134567) is indexed + images online at [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134567](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134567).

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** The Virginia Gazette (Williamsburg/Richmond) was published during the Revolution and is the key newspaper for this period. It carried military appointment notices, loyalist property confiscation notices, runaway servant and enslaved person notices, and family announcements.
- **Where held:** The Colonial Williamsburg Foundation and the Library of Virginia hold microfilm copies. Digital images are available through Accessible Archives and some issues through Chronicling America (Library of Congress, free).
- **Content value:** The Gazette named officers, reported troop movements, published legal notices of estate administrations, and named Loyalists whose property was seized — all genealogically significant.

### Immigration/emigration records

- **Context for this period:** Immigration into Virginia essentially stopped during the war years; emigration out of Virginia during this period was primarily internal — families moving westward into Kentucky County and beyond. These movements appear in county deed records, county court order books (road petitions, land entries), and militia musters in successive counties.
- **Post-war naturalization:** Virginia had no formal naturalization infrastructure yet during the war; those who had been British subjects before 1776 automatically became Virginia citizens. German immigrants in the Shenandoah Valley who arrived pre-war may be traced through Lutheran and Reformed church records and county deed records.

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783 (ID 1945678); Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929 (ID 1598230); Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900 (ID 1734285); Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850 (ID 1456723); Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920 (ID 2134567) | Free |
| Fold3 | NARA pension files and service records (RG 15, RG 93) digitized and indexed | Subscription |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (earliest surviving Virginia census is 1800); various military indexes | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers including Virginia Gazette microfilm | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery memorial transcriptions | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Original service records (RG 93), pension files (RG 15) — request or visit in person | Free (in-person); fee for copies |

**Coverage of this survey:** Volume_search returned 3 digitized volumes matching Virginia 1775–1800 for the selected record types; this appears to be the complete result set for that query (no nextPageToken was returned and totalResults was 3). The FamilySearch indexed collections list (5 collections from collections_search) represents all collections the tool returned for Virginia — totalForPlace was 5.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Library of Virginia, Richmond | Virginia militia records, Land Office patents/grants, tax lists 1782+, county court records, state pension records, Virginia State Navy records | In-person; many records also on microfilm and increasingly online |
| National Archives (Washington, D.C. / College Park) | Continental Line service records (RG 93), pension/bounty-land files (RG 15) | In-person; request copies online at archives.gov |
| Virginia county courthouses | Original deed books, will books, marriage bonds, order books | In-person or mail; many now microfilmed at Library of Virginia |
| DAR Library (Washington, D.C.) | Compiled service records, grave surveys, lineage papers | In-person; member access; some finding aids online |
| Virginia Baptist Historical Society, Richmond | Baptist church records | In-person; inquire for access |
| Colonial Williamsburg Foundation | Virginia Gazette microfilm | In-person; some digitized |

---

## Records NOT online

The following records are known to exist but are not fully available in any name-indexed online database:

- Virginia militia records (held at Library of Virginia; microfilm exists but indexing is incomplete)
- Virginia State Navy records (published in print; not systematically digitized)
- Most individual Anglican/Episcopal vestry books not yet in collection 1598230
- Original Continental Line muster rolls (RG 93 at NARA; Fold3 has some but not all)
- County-level marriage bonds not yet captured in the FamilySearch land/marriage collection
- Loyalist property confiscation records (held at Library of Virginia)
- Virginia 1783 state census fragments
- Revolutionary War land bounty warrants, 1779–1800 (image group 005301447) — images online but browse-only, 0% indexed

---

## Known record losses

- **1790 federal census for Virginia: destroyed.** The British burned Washington in 1814, destroying the Virginia 1790 census returns. The 1782–1783 county personal property tax lists are the primary substitute and survive almost intact at the Library of Virginia. This is confirmed in the FamilySearch Wiki search result at [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands).
- **Individual county courthouse losses:** Some Virginia county courthouses suffered record losses from fire, flood, or the Civil War (notably in 1865). The extent varies county by county — before spending significant research time on a specific county, check the "Virginia County Records" article at the Library of Virginia or FamilySearch Wiki for that county's specific loss history.
- **No known systematic destruction** of the Library of Virginia's militia or Land Office holdings, which remain largely intact.

---

## Research tips

- **Start with pension files, not service records.** Revolutionary War pension application files (NARA RG 15, accessible through Fold3) are far richer than service records: surviving pensions contain sworn affidavits describing the veteran's unit, officer names, battles, age, birthplace, family members, and neighbors who vouched for him. A widow's pension file often adds her maiden name, marriage date, and children's names. Service records confirm enlistment but rarely add genealogical detail. See [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War).
- **Use the 1782–1783 tax lists as your baseline census.** Since the 1790 Virginia federal census was destroyed, these tax lists are the only systematic early enumeration for Virginia. They list the head of household in each county and are the best tool for locating where a family was living at the end of the war.
- **Search both Continental Line and militia records.** Many Virginia men served in both at different times. Continental records are at NARA; militia records are at the Library of Virginia. A man not found in one may appear in the other.
- **Bounty land warrants link veterans to geography.** The Virginia Military District of Ohio bounty land warrants (image group 005301447; browse-only) and the Library of Virginia's warrant/survey records identify veterans who claimed land — and the warrant often names the county of residence at the time of application, a key locating clue. output.text_response:
# Locality Guide: New Orleans, Orleans Parish, Louisiana (1800–1860)

## Jurisdiction Overview

New Orleans was founded by the French in 1718, passed to Spanish control in 1763, briefly reverted to France, then became part of the United States via the Louisiana Purchase in 1803. Louisiana achieved statehood in 1812. The city and Orleans Parish are coextensive. Louisiana is uniquely governed by civil law (Napoleonic Code) rather than English common law, and organized into **parishes** rather than counties.

---

## Known Record Losses — The Disasters Question

This is the heart of your question. Here is what is known:

### The 1788 and 1794 Fires
Two catastrophic fires burned through the French Quarter, destroying most of the colonial-era built environment and a significant portion of early civil records. These predate your research period but directly determine what survived into the early 1800s:

- **Lost:** Many French colonial-era civic records, some early church register volumes, miscellaneous government papers
- **Survived (key point):** The **St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers** survived in substantial form — baptisms, marriages, and burials run from 1731 to the present, with gaps concentrated in fire-affected periods
- **Survived (key point):** A significant portion of **notarial records** survived — the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds over **30 million pages** of notarial acts dating to 1734

### Yellow Fever Epidemics
Recurring epidemics (1817, 1822, 1832, and especially 1853 — which killed ~8,000–12,000 people) overwhelmed recordkeeping. Burial registers from epidemic years may be incomplete or hastily kept.

### Flooding
Periodic flooding damaged courthouse storage, particularly paper records in low-lying areas. The FamilySearch Wiki notes this as a recurring threat, though specific losses in the 1800–1860 period are not fully enumerated.

### Substitute Sources for What Was Lost

| What Was Lost or Damaged | Substitute Source | Where Held |
|---|---|---|
| Missing civil vital records (no statewide system in this period) | St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers | Archdiocese of New Orleans; FamilySearch microfilm |
| Gaps in church registers | Notarial marriage contracts | New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center |
| Missing probate/succession records | Notarial successions (wills, inventories, tutorships) | New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center |
| Lost civic records from fire period | Cabildo records (Spanish colonial governing body) | Louisiana Historical Center, Old U.S. Mint |
| General record gaps | Federal census (1810, 1820, 1830, 1840, 1850, 1860) | FamilySearch; Ancestry |
| Missing burial records | Newspaper death notices | Newspapers.com; Tulane University |

---

## Available Record Types

### Church Records (Primary "Vital Records" for This Period)
Louisiana had **no mandatory statewide civil registration** during most of the 1800–1860 period. Church sacramental registers are the primary vital records:

- **St. Louis Cathedral:** Baptisms, marriages, burials from 1731 (with gaps)
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (collection 1612905) — ~987,000 records with ~493,000 images, indexed and searchable by name
- **Language:** French (pre-1803), Spanish (1769–1803 overlap), English (after 1803 — though French continued in Catholic records for years)
- **Critical note:** Records of enslaved people and free people of color appear in sacramental registers, often in separate sub-registers

### Notarial Records (Unique to Louisiana — The Survivor Story)
This is the **single most important record class** for New Orleans research and a major survival story against the fire losses:

- **What they contain:** Successions (probate equivalents), wills, marriage contracts, property sales, emancipations, slave transactions, business partnerships, tutorships, mortgage agreements, powers of attorney
- **Volume:** Over 30 million pages
- **Date range:** From 1733 (colonial records from 1718)
- **Where held:**
  - Post-1803 records → **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center**
  - French colonial (1718–1769) and Spanish colonial (1769–1803) → **Louisiana Historical Center, Old U.S. Mint**
- **Critical access quirk:** Records are organized by **notary name and date**, NOT by party name. You must know an approximate date and the notary's name to locate a record

### Census Records
- Federal censuses: 1810, 1820, 1830, 1840 (heads of household), 1850, 1860 (all named individuals)
- Slave schedules: 1850 and 1860 (age/sex/description, not names, under enslaver's name)
- Mortality schedules: 1850 and 1860 — particularly valuable given epidemic mortality

### Probate / Succession Records
- Louisiana term: "Successions" (civil law, not probate)
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984" (collection 2078341) — ~456,000 records with ~228,000 images
- Search **both** the court succession records and notarial records for any individual

### Passenger Lists (New Orleans as Major Port of Entry)
New Orleans was the **second-largest U.S. port of entry** after New York. Massive immigration from France, Spain, Germany, Ireland, and the Caribbean passed through here:
- Manifests available on Ancestry and partially on FamilySearch; NARA RG 36 holds originals

### Newspapers
The city had active French-language and bilingual press. Death notices, marriage announcements, estate auction notices, and legal notices are valuable supplements:
- **Newspapers.com** (subscription); Tulane University's Louisiana Research Collection

---

## Repository Guide

### Online
| Repository | Key Collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Church Records 1718–1925 (collection 1612905); Parish Marriages 1837–1957 (1798054); Probate Records 1756–1984 (2078341); Death Index 1819–1964 (1543892) | Free |
| Ancestry | Federal census; New Orleans passenger lists; military records | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military service records and pension files | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Historical New Orleans newspapers | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery inscriptions | Free |

### Physical Repositories
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | 30M+ pages of notarial acts, post-1803 |
| Louisiana Historical Center (Old U.S. Mint) | French & Spanish colonial notarial records; Cabildo records |
| Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge | Territorial/early state records, militia, succession records |
| City Archives, New Orleans Public Library | Orleans Parish tax records, city council minutes |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives | Original St. Louis Cathedral registers |
| NARA Southeast Region, Atlanta | Federal court records, naturalization, passenger list originals |
| Historic New Orleans Collection | Manuscripts, free people of color records, plantation records |
| Tulane University / Amistad Research Center | African American records, historical newspapers |

---

## Key Research Tips

1. **Notarial records are the foundation, not a supplement.** Because Louisiana used civil law, notaries documented births (via baptismal contracts), marriages (marriage contracts), property transfers, wills, and successions — not county courthouses. Always search the Notarial Archives alongside church registers.

2. **Records are organized by notary, not by party name.** To find a notarial record, you need an approximate date and the notary's name. Consult finding aids at the Notarial Archives Research Center.

3. **Three language layers.** Records run in French (pre-1803), Spanish (1769–1803 overlap), and English (post-1803 — though French continued in Catholic records for some years). If you cannot find a record in English, search in French.

4. **"Parish" means two different things.** The civil parish (government unit) ≠ the ecclesiastical parish (church unit). They do not align geographically.

5. **For enslaved and free Black ancestors:** The Catholic sacramental registers and notarial manumission records are far more informative than census slave schedules. The Amistad Research Center at Tulane and the Historic New Orleans Collection hold specialized materials.

6. **Check neighboring parishes:** Jefferson, St. Bernard, and St. Tammany parishes border Orleans. Families near boundaries may have records in adjoining parishes.

7. **The bottom line on disasters:** The two record classes that survived the fires most intact — the Cathedral registers and the notarial archives — are the researcher's anchors for the early 1800s. The fires damaged civic records more than church and notarial records. For epidemic burial gaps, turn to newspaper death notices and mortality schedules.

---

The next practical step would be a structured research plan identifying which specific collections to search first for your specific ancestors' names and time frame.

- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the place_population tool for this specific place. Wikipedia records that New Orleans was one of the largest U.S. cities by the 1840s, driven by the cotton and sugar trade and the Mississippi River port economy.
- **Economy:** Port trade, cotton and sugar commerce, banking, shipping, slave trading. The city was the entry point for a massive wave of immigration from France, the Caribbean, Germany, and Ireland.
- **Ethnic composition:** Creoles (French and Spanish colonial ancestry), enslaved African Americans, free people of color (gens de couleur libres), recent French and Spanish immigrants, Anglo-American migrants from the eastern U.S., German immigrants (especially post-1848), Irish immigrants.
- **Religious denominations:** Predominantly Roman Catholic (St. Louis Cathedral was the dominant institution). Protestant denominations arrived in greater numbers after 1803. Jewish congregations were present by the 1820s.

The territory covered by this guide passed through a clear temporal succession of sovereignties:

- **French colonial period (1718–1769):** Records created under French civil law and the Catholic Church
- **Spanish colonial period (1769–1803):** Records created under Spanish civil law; the Cabildo served as the governing body
- **Brief French return (1803):** Louisiana Purchase transferred authority to the United States the same year
- **Territory of Orleans (1804–1812):** U.S. territorial government; New Orleans remained the administrative center
- **State of Louisiana (1812–present):** Louisiana used civil law (Napoleonic Code) rather than English common law — the only U.S. state to do so — and organized into parishes rather than counties

These are three physically separate repositories, not one continuous series.

Here is what the FamilySearch Wiki ("New Orleans Genealogy," [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters)) and Wikipedia confirm:

- **Survived:** The St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers survived in substantial (though not complete) form because the church itself maintained copies or the registers were stored elsewhere. - **Survived:** A significant portion of the notarial records survived — the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds over 30 million pages of notarial acts dating to 1734, according to the FamilySearch Wiki. ### Flooding
