### Census records

- **Federal census:** The first federal census was taken in 1790 and is available for Philadelphia County. The 1800 census is also available. These bracket the epidemic year. The 1790 census establishes who was living in Philadelphia before the epidemic; comparing to 1800 reveals who disappeared. Note: the 1890 federal census was destroyed by fire, but this does not affect the 1790/1800 records.
- **Access:** The 1790 and 1800 federal census schedules are indexed and available on FamilySearch (free) and Ancestry (subscription).
- **No state census:** Pennsylvania did not conduct state-level censuses in this period.
- **Mortality schedules:** The federal mortality schedules did not begin until 1850 and do not cover 1793.
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images for 1790 and 1800 federal censuses.

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills, letters of administration, estate inventories, guardianships.
- **Epidemic relevance:** The autumn of 1793 produced an enormous spike in probate filings in Philadelphia County as families rushed to settle estates of epidemic victims. A researcher whose ancestor died in 1793 should check the Philadelphia County Register of Wills for filings dated August–December 1793.
- **Date range:** Philadelphia County probate records begin with the county's formation (1682) and are continuous.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994" (collection 1999196) — 3.2 million images, 0 indexed records. This is a browse-only image collection. It covers Philadelphia County and must be navigated image by image with no name search.
- **Digitization level:** Browse-only images (images available on FamilySearch, not name-indexed).
- **Where held:** Philadelphia City Archives (originals); Philadelphia Register of Wills.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania is a state-land state; the Penn proprietors, then the Commonwealth, granted land).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The Penn proprietors granted land originally; after the Revolution, the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania's Land Office. The Pennsylvania State Archives holds the original land records (warrants, surveys, patents).
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, warrants, surveys, and patents.
- **Epidemic relevance:** Families who fled the city may have executed deeds rapidly before departure or sold property afterward. The period 1792–1795 may show unusual transaction volume.
- **Where held:** Philadelphia City Archives (deed books); Pennsylvania State Archives (warrants, surveys, patents).
- **Digitization level:** The `wiki_read` calls for Pennsylvania Land and Property returned generic content. The specific digitization status of Philadelphia deed books for this period could not be confirmed from tool results. Physical and microfilm access are confirmed pathways.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** The Revolutionary War (ended 1783) is immediately prior; the Quasi-War with France began 1798. No major land conflict directly touched Philadelphia in 1793.
- **Epidemic relevance:** Military pension files can document a veteran's presence in Philadelphia at this date. If your ancestor was a Revolutionary War veteran who died in 1793, a pension file may exist that names survivors and place of death.
- **Record types:** Revolutionary War service records and pension files (NARA); bounty land warrants.
- **Where held:** NARA (online via Fold3 for service records; pension files are partially digitized).
- **Digitization level:** Revolutionary War pension files — partially indexed + images on Fold3 (subscription); service records indexed on Fold3 and Ancestry.

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** Christ Church Burial Ground (Independence Mall area), Gloria Dei churchyard, St. Peter's churchyard, Society Hill cemeteries, Hebrew cemeteries, and the Potter's Field used for epidemic dead who had no church.
- **Epidemic burials:** The sheer volume of 1793 deaths overwhelmed church graveyards. Many victims were buried in hastily dug graves. Some churchyard sexton records survive and note the epidemic spike.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com) has coverage of the named Philadelphia cemeteries, though pre-1800 burials are sparsely transcribed.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records survive at some churches and are held at the church or the Historical Society of Pennsylvania.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** Philadelphia had several active newspapers in 1793, including the Federal Gazette, General Advertiser (Aurora), and Dunlap's American Daily Advertiser. These papers published daily lists of the dead by name and address during the epidemic — a unique genealogical resource.
- **Where held:** The Library Company of Philadelphia and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania hold original newspaper runs. Digital access is available through Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com, subscription) and Readex's Early American Newspapers database (library access).
- **Content value for 1793:** The daily dead lists published in the Federal Gazette and other papers during August–November 1793 name individual victims by name and sometimes street address. This is a high-priority source for identifying epidemic victims.

### Immigration/emigration records

- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia was itself a major port of entry.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists (Philadelphia Customs), naturalizations (filed in any Pennsylvania court of record before 1906), and declarations of intention.
- **Epidemic relevance:** Immigration into Philadelphia may have paused during the epidemic. Arrivals in late 1793 and 1794 may document family members who came after a breadwinner's death.
- **Where held:** NARA (passenger lists); Pennsylvania State Archives and Philadelphia City Archives (naturalizations).
- **Digitization level:** Early passenger lists (pre-1820) are partially indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch.
- **Note:** Passenger manifests list every person aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents — always examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records

- **Types:** Pennsylvania taxable inhabitants lists (provincial and state); Philadelphia city ward tax assessments.
- **Date range:** Provincial tax lists predate the county's formation. State tax lists are available through the late 18th century.
- **Epidemic relevance:** Comparing tax lists from 1792 and 1794–1795 can identify households that vanished (possible epidemic deaths or permanent departure) or changed (widow listed where a male head of household appeared before).
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives; Philadelphia City Archives; some are microfilmed at FamilySearch.
- **FamilySearch availability:** Not confirmed as indexed online for this specific period from tool results.

### Probate (revisited as epidemic substitute source)

When church burial records are absent or the denomination is unknown, the Philadelphia County Register of Wills for autumn 1793 is the single most productive substitute. The "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994" collection (FamilySearch 1999196, 3.2 million browse-only images) covers this. Navigate to the Philadelphia County series for 1793 and browse the administration bonds and letters.

### Other record types

- **Published histories:** Mathew Carey's account (see Epidemic-specific records) is both a primary source and a finding aid. J. H. Powell's "Bring Out Your Dead: The Great Plague of Yellow Fever in Philadelphia in 1793" (1949, University of Pennsylvania Press) includes a bibliography of archival sources and transcribes portions of the committee minutes.
- **Free African Society records:** The Free African Society (1787) organized Black nurses and gravediggers during the epidemic. Their records, held at the American Philosophical Society, name free Black residents of Philadelphia during the epidemic period. This is a critical source for African American families.
- **Almshouse records:** Philadelphia's almshouse admitted epidemic victims and orphans. Almshouse records (admissions, deaths) are held at the Philadelphia City Archives.
- **Orphans' Court records:** Children orphaned by the epidemic came before the Orphans' Court, which has records at the Philadelphia City Archives documenting guardianship appointments.

## Known record losses

No specific courthouse fire or systematic destruction of Philadelphia County records for this period was identified in the tool results. Philadelphia's records have generally survived well compared to many other early American jurisdictions. The primary "gap" for 1793 is structural — no civil vital registration system existed, not destruction.

A research gap does exist for the free Black community: many free Black residents had no church connection and did not appear in white-congregation burial registers. The Free African Society records at the American Philosophical Society are the primary substitute.

## Research tips

- **Start with the Mathew Carey list.** The appendix to Carey's fourth edition (1793) names epidemic dead. This is the single fastest way to confirm an ancestor's death during the epidemic. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Philadelphia Genealogy," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793)
- **Church burial registers are the core vital record.** There was no civil death registration in 1793. The church burial register of whatever congregation the family attended is the primary death record. The Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania has compiled indexes to many Philadelphia church records. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Philadelphia Genealogy," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records)
- **Check probate immediately.** An ancestor who died in the autumn of 1793 almost certainly generated a probate filing. Browse the Philadelphia County section of FamilySearch collection 1999196 for August–December 1793 entries. The estate file may name a widow, children, and creditors — often the only family unit document for this period.
- **Compare 1790 and 1800 federal censuses.** A name present in 1790 and absent in 1800 from Philadelphia County is a strong indicator of epidemic death (or permanent out-migration). A widow heading a household in 1800 where a male head appeared in 1790 suggests the husband died between those dates, consistent with the 1793 epidemic.
- **Search neighboring counties for refugees.** Thousands fled Philadelphia in summer 1793. Church registers and tax lists in Delaware, Montgomery, Chester, and Bucks counties may document family members who left and either died there or returned. If they died while in refuge, the death record will be in the host county, not Philadelphia.
- **Philadelphia newspapers name the dead daily.** The Federal Gazette and other Philadelphia papers published lists of the dead by name and street address during August–November 1793. This is a high-priority source and provides address-level precision. Access via Newspapers.com, Readex Early American Newspapers (library database), or the Library Company of Philadelphia.
- **For Quaker ancestors:** The single digitized volume found for this period is the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes (FamilySearch image group 001188322, 1750–1800, browse-only). Quaker vital registers (births, deaths, marriages maintained by each Monthly Meeting) are separate and are held at the Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College.
- **For Black ancestors:** The Free African Society records at the American Philosophical Society are essential. Richard Allen's and Absalom Jones's accounts of their community's epidemic service name specific individuals.
- **Naming customs:** The FamilySearch Wiki Pennsylvania Naming Customs page returned only generic content in this survey. German families in Philadelphia commonly used a given name plus a middle name (Rufname), where the child was called by the second name — an ancestor named "Johann Georg" may appear in records simply as "George." Anglo families used both given and inherited surnames.
- **The epidemic split families geographically.** Some household members fled; others stayed. A single family's records for 1793 may span Philadelphia city records (for those who stayed) and rural county records (for those who fled). Research the full household, not just the head of household.
- **Efficient sequence:** (1) Mathew Carey's published list; (2) Philadelphia County probate 1793 in FamilySearch collection 1999196 (browse-only); (3) church burial register for the family's denomination; (4) Philadelphia newspapers 1793; (5) 1790 and 1800 federal censuses; (6) Committee of 1793 minutes and Bush Hill records at HSP and Philadelphia City Archives.

## The Central Challenge: Courthouse Destruction

The Great Chicago Fire (October 8-10, 1871) destroyed the Cook County Courthouse, wiping out most pre-fire official records — deeds, birth/death registers, court files (including naturalizations), probate records, and tax rolls. This is the defining constraint for all pre-1871 Chicago genealogy research.

---

## What Survived and Where to Find It

### Federal Census Records (Fully Intact)
The 1850, 1860, and 1870 federal census schedules survived because originals were kept in Washington, D.C. **Start with the 1870 census** (bracketing the fire) and the 1880 census to track where the family resettled. Note: the 1890 census was destroyed in Washington in 1921, creating a national gap.

- Available free on FamilySearch; also on Ancestry

### Church Records — The Primary Vital Record Substitute
**Cook County Church Records, 1833–1925** (~285,000 records) on FamilySearch (Collection ID 1803978) — contains pre-fire baptisms, marriages, and burials from parishes that survived or kept off-site duplicates. **Identify the family's denomination before assuming records are lost.**

- Catholic parishes: Archdiocese of Chicago, Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives
- Lutheran (German, Swedish, Norwegian), Methodist, Episcopal, Baptist, Jewish congregations all active in this era

### Chicago Tribune, October–November 1871 Issues
Survivor lists, death notices, and "seeking missing relatives" notices published immediately after the fire. **Browse these issues systematically** — name indexes are incomplete for this specific period. Available on Newspapers.com and ProQuest Historical Newspapers.

### Chicago Relief and Aid Society Records ⭐
One of the most genealogically unique sources from the disaster — names thousands of displaced families with family composition and nationality. **Held physically at the Chicago History Museum.** Contact their research services before visiting.

### Burnt Record Act Re-Recordings (1872)
Illinois law required property owners to re-register lost deeds. These re-recordings often include the original transaction date and prior grantors — a window into pre-fire property history. **Held at the Cook County Recorder of Deeds** (partially online via county systems, not on major genealogy platforms).

### Chicago Title and Trust Company Insurance Records
Documents pre-fire property ownership. **Held physically at the Chicago History Museum.**

### City Directories
Run from the 1840s through and after the fire — the best tool for tracking a family's address across the disaster. Held at the **Newberry Library**; many also on Ancestry.

### Federal Military Records (Fully Intact)
Civil War service records and pension files were in Washington — unaffected by the fire. Pension files often contain names of wife and children, birthplace, and immigration details. Available on Fold3; request naturalization files from USCIS Genealogy Program.

### Post-Fire County Vital Records
The county resumed registration immediately after the fire:
- **Birth Certificates, 1871–1940** (~1.45M records) — FamilySearch Collection ID 2024189
- **Death Records, 1871–1947** (~980K records) — FamilySearch Collection ID 1913456

---

## Research Tips for Fire-Affected Families

1. **Start with the 1870 census** to place the family just before the fire, then the 1880 census to see where they resettled.
2. **Check the church records on FamilySearch** before assuming pre-fire vital records are gone — many parishes outside the fire zone kept records that survive.

# Locality Guide: Chicago, Cook County, Illinois (1860–1890, centered on the Great Fire of October 1871)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** Cook County was established in 1831; Chicago was incorporated as a city in 1837.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Chicago
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Cook County, Illinois
- **Population during period:** Chicago grew from roughly 110,000 in 1860 to approximately 300,000 by 1870, and then to over 500,000 by 1880 — one of the fastest-growing cities in American history. Population figures were not returned by the place_population tool for this query.
- **Economy:** Meatpacking, railroads, lumber, grain trading, manufacturing, and commerce. Chicago was the rail hub of the Midwest.
- **Ethnic composition:** Large communities of Irish, German, Swedish, Norwegian, Polish, Bohemian (Czech), and native-born American settlers. Immigration accelerated after the fire, as reconstruction drew laborers from across Europe.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic, Lutheran (multiple synods — German, Swedish, Norwegian), Methodist, Episcopal, Presbyterian, Baptist, Jewish congregations.
- **Key historical events:** The Great Chicago Fire, October 8-10, 1871 — approximately 300 killed, more than 100,000 left homeless, and roughly 3.3 square miles destroyed, including the Cook County Courthouse and most of the city's official records.

## Boundary changes

- Cook County boundaries were stable throughout this period.
- Chicago's city limits expanded substantially during the 1850s-1880s as the city annexed surrounding townships. Records for families living just outside the 1871 city limits may be held under the township rather than the city.
- No parent-jurisdiction split applies — Cook County existed throughout the entire period.

## The Great Fire: Record Loss — the central fact for this research

The fire destroyed the Cook County Courthouse on October 9, 1871. The courthouse housed deeds, birth and death registers, court records (including naturalization records), probate files, and tax rolls. This is the defining constraint for all pre-1871 Chicago genealogy.

**What survived:**
- The federal census schedules for 1850, 1860, and 1870 survived because the originals were held in Washington, D.C., not in Chicago. The 1870 Chicago enumeration is fully intact.
- City directories from the 1840s onward survived and are held at the Newberry Library.
- Church registers from parishes that were outside the fire zone, or that kept duplicate records off-site, survived in part.
- Insurance company records, particularly the Chicago Title and Trust Company collection, became critical substitutes for property ownership documentation.
- Federal military records (service records, pension files) were in Washington and were unaffected.

**The Burnt Record Act of 1872:** Illinois passed this act to reconstruct property records. It required property owners to re-register their deeds. These re-recordings are the primary substitute for pre-fire deed records and are held at the Cook County Recorder of Deeds.

Source: Wikipedia, "Great Chicago Fire," https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire; FamilySearch Wiki, "Cook County, Illinois Genealogy — Record Loss and the Great Fire," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki did not return the Illinois Vital Records page in a readable form during this survey. The collections_search results show Cook County birth certificates beginning 1871 and death records beginning 1871 — the fire year marks the effective start of surviving records at the county level, though pre-fire records were being kept locally before that. Illinois did not have statewide registration until 1916; county-level registration preceded it but was inconsistently observed.
- **What exists on FamilySearch:**
  - Illinois, Cook County, Birth Certificates, 1871-1940 — collection ID 2024189, approximately 1,450,000 records (indexed + images)
  - Illinois, Cook County, Death Records, 1871-1947 — collection ID 1913456, approximately 980,000 records (indexed + images)
  - Illinois, Cook County, Marriage Records, 1871-1920 — collection ID 1756321, approximately 620,000 records (indexed + images)
- **Pre-fire vital records:** Effectively destroyed. Substitute with church records (see below) and census mortality schedules.
- **Where held:** Cook County Clerk's office (originals); FamilySearch (digitized post-1871 records).

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic, Lutheran (German and Scandinavian synods), Methodist, Episcopal, Presbyterian, Baptist, Jewish.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations. Some denominations also maintained school and membership rolls.
- **What exists on FamilySearch:** Illinois, Cook County, Chicago, Church Records, 1833-1925 — collection ID 1803978, approximately 285,000 records (indexed + images). This collection spans the pre- and post-fire period and is one of the most important sources for pre-1871 vital events.
- **Where held:**
  - Archdiocese of Chicago, Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives (Catholic parish registers) — in-person and correspondence access.
  - FamilySearch has microfilmed many Cook County church registers.
  - Parishes that survived the fire retain their own registers; those in the fire zone may have lost originals, making FamilySearch microfilm the only surviving copy.
- **Language:** German records common for Lutheran and Catholic congregations serving German-speaking immigrants; Scandinavian-language records for Norwegian and Swedish Lutheran parishes.
- **Critical note:** Church records are the primary substitute for pre-fire civil vital records. Identifying the denomination and specific parish a family attended is essential before assuming records are lost.

### Census records

- **Federal census:** 1850, 1860, and 1870 schedules all survived (originals in Washington). The 1880 census is also fully available. The 1890 federal census was largely destroyed by fire in Washington in 1921 — only fragments survive nationally, and Chicago is among the lost portions.
- **Mortality schedules:** The 1870 mortality schedule records deaths in the year preceding the census (June 1869 – May 1870) — this predates the fire and can name individuals who died in that window.
- **State census:** Illinois took state censuses in 1855 and 1865; these can help locate families between federal enumerations and are held at the Illinois State Archives.
- **Access:** 1850, 1860, 1870, and 1880 federal census schedules are indexed and online at FamilySearch and Ancestry. The Illinois state censuses are partially available online.

### Probate and court records

- **Pre-fire:** Probate files and court records including naturalization declarations were destroyed in the 1871 fire. There is no reconstruction equivalent for these records — they are simply gone.
- **Post-fire:** Cook County Circuit Court resumed operations immediately after the fire. Post-1871 naturalizations, probate filings, and court proceedings are held at the Cook County Circuit Court Clerk's office.
- **Substitute:** For pre-fire property and estate matters, the Burnt Record Act re-recordings, city directories, and insurance records are the best substitutes.
- **Digitization level:** 2 digitized volumes appear in FamilySearch volume_search for this place and period: imageGroupNumber 009982110 (38 images, 1865-1871, pre-fire court records, reconstructed copies — browse-only, 0% name-indexed) and 009982111 (112 images, 1871-1880, post-fire property re-recordings — 41% name-indexed, not full-text searchable).
- **Where held:** Cook County Circuit Court Clerk; Illinois Regional Archives Depository at Northeastern Illinois University (IRAD-NEIU) for older county records.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Federal rectangular survey (Illinois is a federal-land state).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (BLM-GLO) issued original patents; subsequent transfers were recorded at the Cook County Recorder of Deeds.
- **Burnt Record Act re-recordings:** Property owners who lost their deeds to the fire re-registered them under the 1872 act. These re-recordings are at the Cook County Recorder of Deeds and are a critical source for establishing pre-fire property ownership.
- **Insurance company records:** The Chicago Title and Trust Company collection at the Chicago History Museum documents pre-fire property ownership and is among the most important substitute sources.
- **Digitization level:** The 112-image post-fire property re-recording volume (imageGroupNumber 009982111, 41% name-indexed) is the main FamilySearch digitized land-adjacent resource for this period.
- **Where held:** Cook County Recorder of Deeds; Chicago History Museum (insurance records); BLM-GLO website (original federal patents, online, free).

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861-1865) — many Chicago men served in Illinois regiments. This is particularly important for families present in Chicago in 1861-1865 and who may have subsequently been affected by the fire.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants — all held at the National Archives (NARA), Washington, D.C. These were unaffected by the Chicago fire.
- **Access:** Civil War service records and pension files are available on Fold3 (subscription) and partially on Ancestry. Illinois regimental records are also at the Illinois State Archives.
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images online (Fold3, Ancestry).

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** Graceland Cemetery (founded 1860), Rosehill Cemetery (founded 1859), and Oak Woods Cemetery survived the fire and hold burials from the period.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com) has significant Chicago cemetery coverage, including transcriptions from Graceland and Rosehill. BillionGraves also covers some Chicago cemeteries.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records at each cemetery; contact individual cemetery offices for pre-digital burial registers.
- **Fire victims:** The fire killed approximately 300 people. Cemetery burial registers from October-November 1871 are the most direct source for fire deaths — not all deaths were formally registered in the immediate aftermath.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** The Chicago Tribune, founded 1847, survived the fire (the Tribune building was damaged but the paper continued publication). The Chicago Tribune published extensive lists of fire victims, relief applicants, and survivors in its October-November 1871 issues — these are among the most genealogically valuable records of the disaster.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com and ProQuest Historical Newspapers hold digitized Chicago Tribune archives. The Chicago History Museum holds original physical issues and microfilm. The Newberry Library also holds extensive newspaper microfilm.
- **Content value:** Post-fire issues (October-November 1871) contain survivor lists, relief distribution lists, death notices, and notices of people seeking missing relatives. These are not consistently indexed by name — browsing is required for the immediate fire period.
- **Digitization level:** Chicago Tribune archives are indexed online via ProQuest (institutional access) and partially via Newspapers.com (subscription). The specific October-November 1871 fire-period issues may require browsing.

### Immigration and emigration records

- **Relevant ports:** Chicago is an inland city — immigrants arrived primarily through New York (Castle Garden, pre-1892; Ellis Island, 1892 onward), Baltimore, Philadelphia, New Orleans, or Quebec, then traveled by rail or Great Lakes steamship to Chicago.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests (NARA, via Ancestry and FamilySearch); naturalization declarations filed in Cook County Circuit Court (pre-fire records destroyed; post-fire records at the Circuit Court Clerk); Declaration of Intention and Petition for Naturalization (post-1906 centralized at NARA via the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services Genealogy Program).
- **Content note:** Passenger manifests record all persons aboard, including infants and children. When researching a family that immigrated to Chicago, examine the full manifest page — siblings and parents traveling together are all listed.
- **Where held:** NARA (passenger lists); Ancestry and FamilySearch (digitized, indexed); Cook County Circuit Court Clerk (post-1871 naturalizations).
- **Digitization level:** Pre-1906 passenger lists: indexed + images on Ancestry and FamilySearch. Post-1906 naturalization files: physical at NARA, request via USCIS Genealogy Program.

### Tax records

- **Pre-fire:** Cook County tax rolls were in the Courthouse and were destroyed in 1871.
- **Post-fire:** Tax records resumed immediately. Post-1871 county tax records are held at the Cook County Assessor's office and the Illinois State Archives.
- **Substitute value:** Pre-fire tax records do not survive; the 1870 federal census (which survived) is the best substitute for placing a person in Chicago just before the fire.

### City directories

- **Date range:** Chicago city directories survive from the 1840s onward through the fire period and beyond.
- **Where held:** The Newberry Library holds one of the strongest collections of pre- and post-fire Chicago city directories. Many are also available on Ancestry.
- **Research value:** City directories list heads of household by name with street address and occupation. They are the single most useful tool for placing a family in Chicago in the years between census enumerations and can establish presence before and after the fire.
- **Digitization level:** Many directories are digitized and browsable on Ancestry; some are indexed by name.

### Relief records

- **Chicago Relief and Aid Society:** This organization distributed relief to fire survivors beginning October 1871. Its records name thousands of families who received aid, with address, family composition, and nationality. This is a genealogically unique record class created specifically by the disaster.
- **Where held:** The Chicago History Museum holds the Chicago Relief and Aid Society records.
- **Digitization level:** Physical only — requires in-person visit or correspondence with the Chicago History Museum.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Cook County Birth Certificates 1871-1940 (~1.45M records); Cook County Death Records 1871-1947 (~980K records); Cook County Marriage Records 1871-1920 (~620K records); Cook County Church Records 1833-1925 (~285K records); 2 digitized volumes (pre-fire court records, post-fire property re-recordings) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census (1850, 1860, 1870, 1880); city directories; passenger lists; Civil War records | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Civil War service records and pension files | Subscription |

| ProQuest Historical Newspapers | Chicago Tribune full archive | Institutional |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery transcriptions for Graceland, Rosehill, Oak Woods | Free |
| BLM-GLO | Federal land patents | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search for Chicago returned 2 digitized volumes total — these are the complete results, not a truncated page. The collections_search returned 4 Illinois-level collections. These represent FamilySearch's digitized holdings; the Newberry Library, Chicago History Museum, and IRAD-NEIU hold substantial additional physical and microfilmed material not reflected here.

### Physical repositories

| Chicago History Museum | Chicago Title and Trust Company insurance records; Chicago Relief and Aid Society records (1871); photographs; newspapers; personal papers | In-person research room; contact for appointments |
| Newberry Library | City directories (1840s onward); maps; manuscripts; Cook County genealogical resources | In-person; some digitized holdings online |
| Cook County Clerk's Office | Vital records (births, marriages, deaths) from 1871 | In-person; mail request; some online |

| Illinois State Archives (Springfield) | State census (1855, 1865); state-level records | In-person; some online |
| NARA Great Lakes Region (Chicago) | Federal records including census originals (for in-person consultation) | In-person |

## Records NOT online

- Chicago Relief and Aid Society survivor and relief records (1871) — Chicago History Museum, physical only
- Chicago Title and Trust Company insurance records — Chicago History Museum, physical only
- Burnt Record Act re-recordings — Cook County Recorder of Deeds (partially online via county systems; not on major genealogy platforms)
- Pre-1871 church registers that survived the fire in physical form — held at individual parishes or the Archdiocesan archives; not consistently digitized

- Illinois state censuses (1855, 1865) — partially online but not fully indexed

## Known record losses

- **Cook County Courthouse fire, October 9, 1871:** Destroyed pre-fire deeds, birth and death registers, court records (including naturalization declarations and naturalizations), probate files, and tax rolls. This is total loss for most county-level records predating the fire.
- **Substitute sources for pre-fire period:**
  - 1870 federal census (survived in Washington)
  - 1860 and 1850 federal census schedules
  - Church records from parishes outside the fire zone or with off-site duplicates

  - Federal military records (pension files, service records — unaffected, held in Washington)
  - Passenger arrival manifests at NARA
- **1890 federal census:** Destroyed nationally by a 1921 fire in Washington — this affects all U.S. research for that year, not just Chicago. The 1880 and 1900 censuses bracket the gap.

- **Start with the 1870 census** (which survived intact) to place the family in Chicago immediately before the fire, then use the 1880 census to confirm where they resettled after it. This bracket is the most reliable frame for fire-era research.
- **The Chicago Tribune's October-November 1871 issues are essential.** They contain survivor lists, death notices, and missing-persons notices published in the immediate aftermath. Browse these issues systematically rather than relying on name indexes, which are incomplete for this specific period. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Cook County, Illinois Genealogy — Record Loss and the Great Fire," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire)
- **The Chicago Relief and Aid Society records at the Chicago History Museum name thousands of fire survivors** with family composition and nationality. This is the closest thing to a fire-survivor list that exists. Contact the Chicago History Museum research services before visiting.
- **Identify the family's church before assuming records are lost.** The Cook County Church Records collection on FamilySearch (1833-1925, ~285,000 records) contains pre-fire baptism, marriage, and burial entries from parishes that survived or whose registers were duplicated off-site. - **Search the Burnt Record Act re-recordings for property owners.** If your ancestor owned property in Chicago before 1871, they were required by the 1872 act to re-register their deed. - **City directories at the Newberry Library are the best pre-fire population source** after the census. They run from the 1840s through the fire and resume immediately after, making it possible to track a family's address across the disaster. Many are also on Ancestry.
- **Federal records were unaffected.** Civil War pension files, passport applications, and naturalization records filed in federal court before 1871 survive in full at NARA. If a Chicago ancestor served in the Civil War, his pension file may contain pre-fire family information — names of wife and children, birthplace, and immigration details.
- **Don't overlook the 1870 mortality schedule.** It records deaths between June 1869 and May 1870, providing names, ages, and causes of death for Chicago residents who died in the year before the fire.
- **Post-fire reconstruction created new records.** Insurance claims, relief applications, and property re-registrations all generated documentation in 1871-1873 that names family members and describes pre-fire circumstances. These reconstruction records are as genealogically valuable as the records they replaced.
- **Repository note from the FamilySearch Wiki:** Key repositories include the Newberry Library (city directories, maps, manuscripts), the Chicago History Museum (insurance records, photographs, personal papers), IRAD-NEIU (Cook County records post-1871), the Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives (Catholic parish registers), and the Cook County Clerk's office (vital records from 1871 onward). output.text_response:
Here is the locality guide returned by the specialist agent:

---

# Locality Guide: Louisiana (French Colonial Period, 1700–1803)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Established:** French colonial Louisiana was claimed in 1682 by La Salle; permanent settlement and record-keeping began from 1699 onward. New Orleans was founded in 1718.
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans (seat of the Superior Council and Catholic ecclesiastical authority)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** New France (France), then Spanish Louisiana from 1762–1803
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholicism was the *only* legally recognized church under the Code Noir — Protestant worship was prohibited. All vital events were recorded exclusively by Catholic priests.
- **Key historical events:** Founding of New Orleans (1718); Code Noir enforced (1724); France cedes western Louisiana to Spain (1762); Spanish administration begins (1769); Louisiana Purchase (1803)

---

## Boundary Changes — Critical Research Trap

The colony passed through three administrations:

- **1699–1762 — French Louisiana:** Superior Council was the judicial/administrative body. Records split between Louisiana and France (ANOM, Aix-en-Provence).
- **1762/1769–1800 — Spanish Louisiana:** Spain received the colony in 1762 but didn't exercise authority until 1769. The Cabildo replaced the Superior Council. Records are in Louisiana, France, and Spain (Archivo General de Indias, Seville).
- **1800–1803 — Brief French retrocession**, then U.S. sovereignty.

**A family active in the 1750s–1780s will have records under two colonial administrations, in French and/or Spanish, in repositories on two continents.**

---

## Available Record Types

### Church Records (Your Foundation)
There was **no civil vital registration** in colonial Louisiana — Catholic sacramental registers ARE the primary record for the entire 1700s.

- **Content:** Baptisms (including enslaved persons), marriages, and burials. Marriage registers often include ages, places of origin, and parents' names — invaluable for tracing immigrant origins.
- **Date range:** From 1720 (St. Louis Cathedral, New Orleans)
- **Language:** French (1700–1769); French and Spanish mixed (1769–1803)
- **Where held:**
  - **FamilySearch Collection 1612905** — "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (~987,654 indexed, searchable records with images) — **start here**
  - **FamilySearch Volume 004330991** — 264 images of sacramental registers, 1720–1803; 0% name-indexed, browse-only, in French/Spanish
  - **Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives** — original registers from 1720 (in-person, by appointment)

### Probate and Court Records
- **Superior Council records** (French, 1714–1769) and **Cabildo records** (Spanish, 1769–1803) contain estate inventories, wills, land concessions, and court proceedings.
- **Where held:**
  - **Louisiana Historical Center** (Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans) — partially digitized
  - **FamilySearch Collection 2078341** — "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984" (~456,789 records with images; colonial period overlap)
  - **FamilySearch Volume 004330992** — 149 images of French colonial Superior Council notarial acts, 1699–1769; browse-only, in French

### Notarial Acts (Marriage Contracts — Exceptional Resource)
- French legal custom made notarial marriage contracts standard practice. These **routinely record the parents' names and home parishes** of both parties — often your only clue to European origins.
- **Where held:** **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** — acts from the 1730s onward; oldest continuous notarial office in North America. In-person research; some digitization ongoing.

### Colonial Census Records
- French colonial census rolls exist for c.1721, 1724, 1726, and 1732. These are household-level administrative counts noting free and enslaved persons, livestock, and crops.
- **Where held:** **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France**; also microfilmed at the Louisiana Historical Center. Not indexed online.

### Land Records
- French long-lot (arpent) system along the Mississippi — entirely different from the post-American rectangular survey.
- **Types:** French concessions, Spanish land grants, notarial acts of sale/mortgage.
- **Where held:**
  - **New Orleans Notarial Archives** — property transactions from the 1730s
  - **Louisiana State Land Office** — Spanish land grant documentation
  - **American State Papers: Public Lands** (HathiTrust, Ancestry) — post-1803 adjudication of colonial-era claims
  - **ANOM (Aix-en-Provence)** — French administrative correspondence on land concessions

### Military Records
- French colonial troop musters/militia rolls; Spanish presidio rosters and pension files.
- **Where held:**
  - **ANOM (Aix-en-Provence)** — French colonial military records
  - **Archivo General de Indias (Seville, Spain)** — Spanish colonial military records for Louisiana, 1769–1803
  - **Fold3.com** — some colonial-era military records (subscription)

### Immigration Records
Key immigrant groups:
- French settlers arriving 1699–1762
- German Coast settlers (Rhine Valley Germans, c.1719–1722)
- Acadian exiles post-1755 (Grand Dérangement)
- African-born enslaved persons (documented in Code Noir baptism records)

**Where held:**
- **ANOM (Aix-en-Provence)** — Company of the Indies passenger and settler lists
- **Centre d'Études Acadiennes, Université de Moncton (Canada)** — premier Acadian genealogy database; connects Louisiana Acadian families to their pre-Deportation Nova Scotia origins

### Enslaved Ancestors
The Code Noir of 1724 mandated Catholic baptism of all enslaved persons. These entries appear in the same sacramental registers as free persons, with the enslaver's name recorded. This is **frequently the only surviving record** for enslaved individuals. Cross-reference with estate inventories and sale records in Superior Council papers.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online Repositories

| Repository | Relevant Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Collection 1612905 (church records, 1718–1925, indexed); Collection 2078341 (probate, 1756–1984); Volume 004330991 (sacramental registers, browse-only); Volume 004330992 (Superior Council notarial acts, browse-only) | Free |
| **Ancestry.com** | Some colonial transcription databases; U.S. Federal Census (post-1803 only) | Subscription |
| **Fold3.com** | Some colonial-era military records | Subscription |
| **PARES (pares.mcu.es)** | Partial online access to Archivo General de Indias (Spanish colonial Louisiana) | Free |
| **anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr** | Some digitized ANOM holdings (French colonial records) | Free |

### Physical Repositories

| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| **Louisiana Historical Center** (New Orleans) | Superior Council records (French colonial); Cabildo records (Spanish colonial) |
| **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** | Notarial acts from the 1730s: marriage contracts, property transactions, wills |
| **Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives** | Original sacramental registers from 1720 |
| **Louisiana State Archives** (Baton Rouge) | Post-1803 state records; some colonial-era transcriptions |
| **ANOM** (Aix-en-Provence, France) | Colonial census rolls, administrative records, military records, Company of the Indies passenger lists |
| **Archivo General de Indias** (Seville, Spain) | Spanish colonial Louisiana records, 1769–1803 |
| **Centre d'Études Acadiennes**, Université de Moncton | Acadian genealogy databases |

---

## Records NOT Online

- French colonial census rolls (1721, 1724, 1726, 1732) — ANOM only
- Bulk of Superior Council court and contract records — largely in-person at Louisiana Historical Center
- Cabildo records — partially digitized but not fully indexed
- Spanish colonial military pension/service records — partial PARES digitization
- Company of the Indies passenger lists — ANOM; not online
- Most pre-1760s notarial acts — New Orleans Notarial Archives, in-person only

---

## Known Record Losses

- The original St. Peter Street Cemetery (French colonial) no longer exists; burials survive only if recorded in sacramental registers.
- Sacramental registers from outlying colonial parishes (Mobile, Natchitoches, Illinois Country posts) have uneven survival.
- Some Superior Council volumes are fragmentary due to water damage.
- Hurricane Katrina (2005) caused damage at some New Orleans repositories — confirm access before visiting.

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with FamilySearch Collection 1612905** ("Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925") — it's the indexed, searchable entry point for the entire colonial era.

2. **Seek notarial marriage contracts.** These often name both parties' parents and home parishes, and are the best route to European origins. New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds these from the 1730s.

3. **Search both colonial administrations.** A family straddling 1762 will have records in both French and Spanish administrative series, in separate repositories — including archives in France and Spain. Plan for both.

4. **For Acadian families:** The Centre d'Études Acadiennes database at the Université de Moncton is the essential starting point; it can supply generations of pre-Louisiana data.

5. **Browse-only volumes require systematic scanning.** Volumes 004330991 and 004330992 on FamilySearch are 0% name-indexed. Use published transcription indexes (e.g., Winston DeVille's compilations of Louisiana colonial marriage contracts and census records) to identify specific volume/page references before browsing.

6. **Language:** French colonial records are in 18th-century French; Spanish colonial records in Spanish (though many local documents remained in French even under Spanish rule). Plan for translation assistance.

7. **Identify the specific parish or settlement** where your ancestor lived — records outside New Orleans (Natchitoches, German Coast, Acadian bayou settlements) are held in different repositories with varying survival rates.

# Locality Guide: Louisiana (French Colonial Period, 1700-1803)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Established:** French colonial Louisiana was claimed in 1682 by La Salle; permanent settlement and record-keeping began in earnest from 1699 onward. New Orleans was founded in 1718.
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans (seat of the Superior Council and Catholic ecclesiastical authority)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** New France (France), then Spanish Louisiana from 1762-1803
- **Population during period:** No census population figures were returned by the tools for this period. Colonial censuses were taken irregularly — notable ones include 1721, 1724, 1726, and 1732 — and are preserved in French and Spanish colonial archives.
- **Economy:** Fur trade, indigo, tobacco, lumber, and later sugar cane; plantation agriculture dependent on enslaved labor
- **Ethnic composition:** French colonists, Canadian voyageurs, Africans (enslaved and free), Native Americans, Acadian exiles (arriving post-1755), German Coast settlers, and Spanish officials and soldiers (after 1762)
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholicism was the only legally recognized church in French Louisiana under the Code Noir. Protestant worship was prohibited; all vital events were recorded exclusively by Catholic priests throughout the colonial period.
- **Key historical events:** Founding of New Orleans (1718); Code Noir enforced (requiring baptism of all enslaved persons); France cedes western Louisiana to Spain by Treaty of Fontainebleau (1762); Spanish colonial administration begins (1769); Louisiana Purchase transfers territory to the United States (1803)

## Boundary changes

The colonial period involves a critical three-way jurisdictional split:

- **1699-1762 — French Louisiana:** Records created under French authority. The Superior Council (Conseil Superieur) was the administrative and judicial authority. Catholic parishes recorded vital events. Administrative records are split between Louisiana (Louisiana Historical Center) and France (Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence).
- **1762/1769-1800 — Spanish Louisiana:** Spain received western Louisiana in 1762 but did not exercise effective authority until 1769. The Spanish Cabildo replaced the Superior Council. Spanish notarial and ecclesiastical record-keeping continued, largely in French for the early decades. Records from this period are held at the Louisiana Historical Center, the New Orleans Notarial Archives, and the Archivo General de Indias (Seville, Spain).
- **1800-1803 — Brief French retrocession**, followed immediately by the Louisiana Purchase and U.S. sovereignty.

**Critical research implication:** A family active in the 1750s-1780s will have records filed under two different colonial administrations, in French and/or Spanish, in repositories on two continents. Do not search only one administrative series.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** There was no civil vital registration in Louisiana during the colonial period. The Catholic Church held exclusive authority over vital record-keeping throughout the 1700s. Civil registration in Louisiana did not begin at the state level; the FamilySearch Wiki pages fetched for this jurisdiction returned only generic content and did not state a specific statewide start date.
- **What exists:** Baptisms, marriages, and burials recorded by Catholic priests from 1720 onward in sacramental registers. St. Louis Cathedral in New Orleans has registers beginning in 1720, per the wiki_search result from the [Louisiana Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records) page.
- **Where held:** Archdiocese of New Orleans archives; FamilySearch has digitized a set of these registers (see FamilySearch collection 1612905, "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925," below).
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** The sacramental registers ARE the primary record for this entire period. There are no civil vital records to substitute; church records are the original source.

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic only (legally mandated under French colonial law and Code Noir). Protestant congregations were not legally permitted until after the Louisiana Purchase.
- **Record types:** Baptisms (including enslaved persons under the Code Noir mandate), marriages, burials, and confirmations. Marriage registers frequently include ages, places of origin, and names of parents — making them particularly valuable for tracing immigrant origins.
- **Where held:**
  - **Archdiocese of New Orleans:** Original registers from 1720
  - **FamilySearch (digitized, browse-only):** Volume imageGroupNumber 004330991 — 264 images of sacramental registers, Archdiocese of New Orleans, covering 1720-1803, in French and Spanish. This volume is 0% name-indexed and is not full-text searchable — it must be browsed image by image.
  - **FamilySearch collection 1612905** ("Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925"): ~987,654 records with images; this is an indexed collection and is searchable by name. It covers the colonial period start date of 1718.
- **Language:** French for French colonial records (1700-1769); a mix of French and Spanish under Spanish administration (1769-1803). Researchers must be able to read both languages or use a translator for the original documents.

### Census records

- **Colonial enumerations:** French colonial census rolls exist for several years (c.1721, 1724, 1726, 1732) and are held at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM) in Aix-en-Provence, France, and in transcribed/microfilmed form at the Louisiana Historical Center. These are not federal censuses; they are administrative head counts organized by household, noting enslaved and free persons, livestock, and crops.
- **Federal/national census:** The first U.S. federal census covering Louisiana territory is 1810 (after the 1803 Louisiana Purchase). For the colonial period, there is no U.S. federal census to consult.
- **Access:** The colonial census rolls are physical and microfilm records, not indexed online. The Louisiana Historical Center and ANOM are the primary holders.

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Estate inventories, wills, administrations, guardianships, and contracts recorded by the Superior Council (French period) and the Cabildo (Spanish period). The Superior Council also recorded land concessions and court proceedings.
- **Date range:** Superior Council records begin c.1714 and continue to 1769 when Spain formally took control; Cabildo records run from 1769 to 1803.
- **Where held:**
  - **Louisiana Historical Center** (in the Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans): Holds Superior Council records and has partially digitized them, per the [Louisiana Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records) wiki_search result.
  - **FamilySearch collection 2078341** ("Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984"): ~456,789 records with images; date range begins in 1756 (the colonial period), so this overlaps the French and Spanish eras.
  - **FamilySearch volume 004330992**: 149 images of French colonial notarial acts (Superior Council records), dated 1699-1769, in French. This volume is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — browse-only in French.
- **Note on testate vs. intestate:** Estate inventories were frequently compiled regardless of whether a will existed; for the colonial period, look for both the inventory and any notarial act constituting a will in the Superior Council / notarial records, not in a separate probate court.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** French long-lot (arpent) system along the Mississippi and bayous — entirely different from the rectangular survey system used after American acquisition. Lots ran narrow along waterways with long depth, producing a distinctive settlement pattern.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Under French authority, the Superior Council and the Company of the Indies (Compagnie des Indes) granted land concessions. Under Spain, the Cabildo and Spanish land grant processes applied.
- **Types:** French concessions, Spanish land grants, notarial acts of sale and mortgage, and estate inventories recording real property. After the Louisiana Purchase, Spanish land claims were adjudicated by the U.S. and documented in the American State Papers: Public Lands series.
- **Where held:**
  - **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center**: Holds notarial acts from the 1730s onward — contracts, wills, marriage settlements, and property transactions — per the [Louisiana Land and Property](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants) wiki_search result. This is the oldest continuous notarial office in North America.
  - **Louisiana State Land Office**: Spanish land grant documentation.
  - **American State Papers: Public Lands** (available on HathiTrust and Ancestry): Documents post-1803 adjudication of colonial-era French and Spanish land claims.
  - **ANOM (Aix-en-Provence)**: French administrative correspondence on land concessions.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** The French and Indian War (Seven Years' War, 1754-1763) directly caused France's cession of Louisiana. Colonial militia rosters and troop records exist for the French and Spanish periods.
- **Record types:** French colonial troop musters and militia rolls; Spanish military records (presidio rosters, pension files under Spanish administration).
- **Where held:**
  - **ANOM (Aix-en-Provence)**: French colonial military records
  - **Archivo General de Indias (Seville, Spain)**: Spanish colonial military records for Louisiana, 1769-1803
  - **Louisiana Historical Center**: Some transcribed and microfilmed militia records
  - **Fold3.com**: Holds some colonial-era military records; access by subscription.

### Cemetery records

- **Colonial-era burials:** Most colonial-era burials were in Catholic cemeteries associated with parishes. St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 in New Orleans (founded 1789) is the oldest extant above-ground cemetery; earlier burials within the French colonial period were in the original St. Peter Street Cemetery (no longer extant).
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (findagrave.com, free) has some entries for surviving colonial-era tombstones, but coverage for 18th-century graves is sparse and fragmentary. Many original burials are unmarked or markers no longer survive.
- **Physical records:** Burial entries in the Catholic sacramental registers (see Church Records above) are often the best surviving record of a colonial-era death and burial.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** The first Louisiana newspaper, the Moniteur de la Louisiane, was founded in 1794 — at the very tail end of the colonial period and under Spanish rule. No French colonial-period newspapers survive from the early 1700s.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State University Libraries (Louisiana Digital Library); Newspapers.com (subscription) for later holdings.
- **Content value:** The 1794-onward papers contain legal notices, estate notices, and some personal announcements, relevant to families active at the transition to U.S. rule.

### Immigration and emigration records

- **Relevant ports and movements:** New Orleans was the primary port of entry for French Louisiana. Key immigrant groups to research include:
  - French settlers arriving 1699-1762 (many recruited by the Company of the Indies)
  - German Coast settlers (Rhine Valley Germans, arriving c.1719-1722)
  - Acadian exiles arriving after 1755 (the Grand Derangement)
  - African-born enslaved persons — documented in slave trade manifests and in the Code Noir baptism records
- **Record types:** Passenger lists for colonial arrivals were kept by the Company of the Indies and French crown; these are held at ANOM. Post-1803 NARA passenger lists begin with the Port of New Orleans series.
- **Where held:**
  - **ANOM (Aix-en-Provence)**: Company of the Indies passenger and settler lists
  - **NARA (Washington, D.C. / Atlanta regional)**: Port of New Orleans passenger lists from 1820 onward (post-colonial, but relevant for continued immigration)
  - **Acadian records**: The Centre d'Etudes Acadiennes at the Universite de Moncton (New Brunswick, Canada) holds the premier Acadian genealogy database (BALSAC / Fichier Origine) for families before and after the Deportation.
- **Content note:** Colonial-era passenger lists record heads of household and sometimes entire families. Cross-reference arrivals with baptism registers to confirm family members who may have been born in transit or shortly after arrival.

### Tax records

- **Types:** Colonial-era tax and tribute lists were compiled as administrative censuses; they are integrated with the colonial census rolls rather than existing as a separate tax-record series in the American sense.
- **Where held:** ANOM and Louisiana Historical Center (with the census and Superior Council records).
- **Substitute value:** The colonial census/enumeration rolls substitute for both census and tax records for this period, listing property, enslaved persons, and household members.

### Other record types

- **Notarial acts (contracts):** The New Orleans Notarial Archives hold acts from the 1730s covering marriage contracts (contrats de mariage), which routinely name the parents of both parties and their places of origin — an extraordinary resource for tracing immigrant origins and family relationships.
- **Code Noir baptism records:** The Code Noir of 1724 required Catholic baptism and instruction for all enslaved persons. These entries appear in the same sacramental registers as free persons, often with the enslaver named as the record's creator or godparent. This is frequently the primary surviving record for enslaved individuals.
- **Published colonial genealogies and local histories:** Works such as Winston DeVille's compilations of Louisiana colonial records (marriage contracts, census transcriptions) and the Conrad/Robichaux Acadian genealogical series have indexed many otherwise browse-only colonial records. Check WorldCat and the FamilySearch Catalog for these titles.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Collection 1612905: "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925" (~987,654 records, indexed + images); Collection 2078341: "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984" (~456,789 records, images); Volume 004330991: Sacramental registers 1720-1803, 264 images, browse-only, French/Spanish; Volume 004330992: Superior Council notarial acts 1699-1769, 149 images, browse-only, French | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census (post-1803 only for Louisiana); some colonial transcription databases | Subscription |
| Fold3.com | Some colonial-era military records | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery transcriptions (sparse for colonial period) | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Louisiana newspapers from 1794 onward | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Port of New Orleans passenger lists (1820+); post-1803 federal records | Free / fee-based reproductions |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 2 digitized volumes matching Louisiana in the 1699-1803 window — these appear to be the complete result set (no nextPageToken returned, totalResults: 2). Four FamilySearch indexed collections were returned for Louisiana overall; not all are filtered to the colonial period specifically (the church records and probate records begin in 1718 and 1756, respectively, which overlap the target period).

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Louisiana Historical Center (Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans) | Superior Council records (French colonial); Cabildo records (Spanish colonial); partially digitized | In-person; some finding aids online |
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | Notarial acts from the 1730s: marriage contracts, property transactions, wills | In-person research room; some records being digitized |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives | Original sacramental registers from 1720 | In-person by appointment |
| Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge) | Post-1803 state records; some colonial-era transcriptions | In-person; some online access |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer — ANOM (Aix-en-Provence, France) | French colonial census rolls, administrative correspondence, military records, Company of the Indies passenger lists | In-person; some digitized at anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr |
| Archivo General de Indias (Seville, Spain) | Spanish colonial Louisiana records, 1769-1803 | In-person; Portal de Archivos Espanoles (PARES) provides partial online access |
| Centre d'Etudes Acadiennes, Universite de Moncton (Canada) | Acadian genealogy databases and family files | In-person and online (partial) |

## Records NOT online

The following categories exist but are not fully available in any online database:

- French colonial census rolls (1721, 1724, 1726, 1732) — ANOM; not indexed online
- The bulk of Superior Council court and contract records — partially held at Louisiana Historical Center; not systematically indexed or digitized
- Cabildo records (Spanish colonial administration, 1769-1803) — Louisiana Historical Center; partially digitized but not fully indexed
- Spanish colonial military pension and service records — Archivo General de Indias; partial PARES digitization but not fully searchable by name for Louisiana
- Company of the Indies passenger and settler lists — ANOM; not generally online
- Notarial acts predating systematic digitization (1730s-1760s) — New Orleans Notarial Archives; in-person only for much of this range

## Known record losses

- The original St. Peter Street Cemetery (French colonial period) no longer exists; burial records for those interred there survive only in the sacramental registers if they were recorded at all.
- Some early sacramental registers from outlying colonial parishes (Mobile, Natchitoches, Illinois Country posts) have been lost or damaged; coverage outside New Orleans is uneven.
- The Louisiana Historical Center holdings suffered from water damage in past decades; some Superior Council volumes are fragmentary.
- Hurricane Katrina (2005) caused damage to some holdings at the Archdiocese of New Orleans and other repositories; researchers should confirm current access before visiting.

## Research tips

- **Catholic registers are your foundation.** For the entire 1700s, there was no civil vital registration in Louisiana — the Catholic sacramental registers are not a substitute, they are the primary record. Begin with FamilySearch collection 1612905 ("Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925"), which is name-indexed, before moving to the browse-only volumes. ([Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records))

- **Marriage contracts in notarial records are exceptional.** French legal custom made a notarial marriage contract (separate from the church marriage register) standard practice for propertied families. These contracts, held at the New Orleans Notarial Archives from the 1730s, routinely record the parents' names and home parishes of both parties — often your only clue to European origins. ([Louisiana Land and Property — Colonial Land Grants](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants))

- **The mid-century jurisdictional split is a research trap.** A family present in the 1750s was under French rule; the same family in the 1770s was under Spanish authority. Their records will appear in different administrative series, potentially in different languages, in different archives — including archives in France and Spain. Plan to search both colonial administrations as a connected trail, not as unrelated record sets.

- **For Acadian families (arriving post-1755):** The Centre d'Etudes Acadiennes database at the Universite de Moncton is the essential starting point; it connects Louisiana Acadian families to their pre-Deportation origins in Nova Scotia and can supply generations of family data before the Louisiana sojourn.

- **Enslaved ancestors:** The Code Noir of 1724 mandated Catholic baptism of all enslaved persons; baptism entries appear in the same registers as free persons. These are often the only surviving record. The enslaver's name is recorded, which can guide further research into estate inventories and sale records within the Superior Council papers.

- **Language of records:** French colonial records are in 17th- and 18th-century French; Spanish colonial records are in Spanish, though many local documents remain in French even under Spanish rule. Latin appears in some sacramental entries. Researchers unfamiliar with these languages should plan for translation assistance or engage a specialist in colonial Louisiana records.

- **Browse-only volumes require systematic scanning.** The two digitized FamilySearch volumes for this period (imageGroupNumbers 004330991 and 004330992) are 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — every image must be opened and read individually. For the notarial acts volume, the records are organized chronologically by notary, not by surname, so a finding aid or published index (such as DeVille's works) is essential before attempting to browse.

- **Published transcription volumes as a starting point:** Genealogist Winston DeVille compiled and published indexes to Louisiana colonial marriage contracts, census records, and other sources. These are available in large genealogical library collections and through WorldCat interlibrary loan, and can point you to the specific notarial act or register volume where a family appears before you visit or request records.

Tracing families in French colonial Louisiana in the 1700s means working with Catholic sacramental registers as the only vital records of the era, supplemented by notarial acts (especially marriage contracts), colonial census rolls, and Superior Council court and estate records. The key complication is that the colony passed from French to Spanish authority around 1762-1769, so records for families active across that boundary are split between two administrative systems — and between archives in Louisiana, France, and Spain. FamilySearch has one indexed, searchable collection of Louisiana church records starting from 1718, plus two browse-only (unindexed, French/Spanish-language) digitized volumes covering sacramental registers and Superior Council notarial acts.

Here is the locality guide returned by the research agent:

---

# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region (1860–1900)

## Jurisdiction Overview

**Primary counties:** Schuylkill, Luzerne, Lackawanna (formed from Luzerne in 1878), Carbon, and Northumberland.

**Key boundary change:** Lackawanna County was created from Luzerne County in **1878**. Events in the Scranton/Carbondale area *before* 1878 are under **Luzerne County** records.

---

## Record Types & Where to Find Them

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- Pennsylvania had **no statewide birth or death registration** before 1906.
- **Marriage records** exist from 1885 on FamilySearch: "Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950" and "Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950."
- For deaths and births before 1906, turn to **church registers, Mine Inspector Reports, and newspaper notices**.

### Church Records *(most critical source)*
- **FamilySearch** holds "Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records" (1708–1985, 1.2M records / 607K images).
- Ethnic parishes are key: Irish, Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, Italian (Catholic), Welsh Congregational/Baptist, Lutheran, Methodist, and Presbyterian.
- Language varies by ethnic parish — records may be in Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, or Latin.
- Undigitized registers: contact the **Diocese of Allentown** (Schuylkill/Carbon) or **Diocese of Scranton** (Luzerne/Lackawanna).

### Census Records
- **Federal censuses:** 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900 (1890 largely destroyed — see below).
- The 1880 census identifies occupations precisely; the 1900 census records immigration year and citizenship status.
- **Mortality schedules** (1860, 1870, 1880) list people who died in the preceding year — a vital substitute for missing death records.

### Occupational Records *(unique to this locality)*
- **Pennsylvania Mine Inspector Reports (1870+):** Name every fatal mining accident victim with age, nationality, and cause of death. Held at the **Pennsylvania State Archives** (Harrisburg). This is the primary death record when no certificate exists.
- **FamilySearch digitized volumes:**
  - Vol. 002240015 — Schuylkill County Mine Worker Employment Cards, 1870–1900 (410 images, 95% name-indexed, full-text searchable) — *start here*
  - Vol. 002240016 — Luzerne County Mine Accident Reports, 1870–1895 (browse-only)
  - Vol. 002240017 — Lackawanna County Colliery Payroll Ledgers, 1878–1900 (browse-only)
- 20 additional digitized volumes in FamilySearch remain to be examined.

### Naturalization Records
- Miners naturalized in county courts; **Schuylkill County naturalization records (1840s–1906)** are at the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- After 1906, check federal court records and USCIS.

### Probate & Court Records
- "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994" (FamilySearch collection 1999196) — 3.2M images, browse-only.
- Originals at county courthouses (Pottsville for Schuylkill; Wilkes-Barre for Luzerne).

### Immigration Records
- Irish/German miners typically arrived through **Philadelphia** (pre-1880).
- Central/Eastern European miners arrived through **New York** (Castle Garden / Ellis Island from 1892).
- Indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch; examine the full manifest page for all family members.

### Newspapers
- **The Miners' Journal** (Pottsville, 1825–present): Reports mining fatalities with names, ages, nationalities, and surviving family. Available on Newspapers.com and on microfilm at the Historical Society of Schuylkill County.

### Cemetery Records
- **Find A Grave** provides headstone photos and transcriptions; coverage varies for smaller ethnic cemeteries.

---

## Key Repositories

| Repository | What's There |
|---|---|
| FamilySearch (free) | Church records, marriages, probate images, employment cards |
| Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) | Mine Inspector Reports (1870+), naturalization records, state military records |
| Historical Society of Schuylkill County (Pottsville) | Miners' Journal microfilm, local mining records, family files |
| Anthracite Heritage Museum (Scranton) | Northern anthracite field records (Luzerne/Lackawanna) |
| Diocese of Allentown Archives | Catholic parish registers, Schuylkill & Carbon Counties |
| Diocese of Scranton Archives | Catholic parish registers, Luzerne & Lackawanna Counties |
